#3233. Disney is now embracing the AI it once fought, from cartoons to finance

An AI-animated kids' show is coming to Disney+ as CEO Josh D'Amaro brings AI into every part of the company.

The Alameda Avenue entrance to the Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, California, in July 2016.

Disney will bring Ozzy Fox, a kids’ series animated with AI tools, to Disney+ in December, Bloomberg reported. Under CEO Josh D’Amaro, it is also using AI in finance, streaming suggestions and its parks, while still guarding its characters.

Disney, which once sued AI companies over its characters, is now putting the technology to work across the company, Bloomberg reported. In December, it will bring Ozzy Fox, a children’s series animated with AI, to Disney+.

Ozzy Fox was made with French startup Animaj, whose tools turn artists’ drawings and text instructions into 3D animation. It first appeared on YouTube in July, where some viewers called it “AI slop”.

The push is led by CEO Josh D’Amaro, who took over this year. A week into his tenure, OpenAI shut down its Sora video app, ending a planned deal for Disney to license its characters to it.

“We’re being very aggressive about exploring emerging technologies,” D’Amaro said at a company event this month.

In September, Disney named Character.AI’s chief executive, Karandeep Anand, as its first CTO. It has since bid $20M for some of the assets of the bankrupt chatbot startup, which could one day let Disney+ users talk to characters.

Disney still guards its characters closely. Rather than license them to AI firms, it has signed a deal letting Adobe build AI models on them under its control.

#3231. The Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder is just $229, the cheapest bean-to-cup espresso machine I’ve ever seen; unfortunately, it looks and acts like it too — no Breville-beater

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At just $229, the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder is the cheapest bean-to-cup I’ve ever seen. It even has a PID controller, built-in timer, and a nice, weighty tamper. Surely this is too good to be true? Well, if you’re a coffee nerd, yes. The grinder is really inconsistent and the steam wand is quite weak — not to mention the pressurized-only portafilters. Could that sweet, sweet price of $229 be enough to convince you, though? I’m not sure it convinced me.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When I saw the price of the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder, my eyes bulged out of my head like a cartoon rabbit being chased by a mountain lion. $229? For an espresso machine… and a grinder? What year is this, 2001?

It’s hard to explain just how cheap $229 is, but I’ll do my best. The entry-level Casabrews Tornado grinder is $139 — and that’s seriously budget. The De’Longhi Stilosa espresso machine is $149 — and, again, that’s seriously budget. So $229 for a grinder and an espresso machine is literally unheard of.

So, how does the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder hold up? Well, it’s $229. That’s all I really have to say. While, yes, this is the cheapest bean-to-cup I’ve ever seen, it performs like it. But this might be enough to make it one of your best espresso machines if you’re on a budget best described as “as close to zero as possible”. Find out the full story in this Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder review.

2 x pressurized portafilters, scoop, tamper, tamping collar, brush

The Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder is $229 from Amazon U.S. and £239 from Amazon U.K. On Amzchef’s website, the Espresso Machine with Grinder is listed as “All-in-One” espresso machine and is $299 rather than $229. The “Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder” is a completely different product with a different screen style — albeit $229, not $299. I've raised this with Amzchef and have been informed it will correct this inconsistency.

They don’t make it easy for us, huh? Anyway, I would buy from Amazon due to the lower price. For ease of searching, the product code is CM1626 — but Amzchef doesn’t list this on its website (for any of its products… just a wonderful, transparent business strategy, I know). The links above are to the Amazon page, not Amzchef’s site.

Opaque pricing aside, the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder is incredibly cheap. As I wrote in my “Pros” section above, it’s almost unbelievably cheap. A bean-to-cup espresso machine for $229? Seriously? Most electric grinders start at $150, like the Casabrews Tornado or Breville Dose Control Pro.

The only machines I’ve tested around the same price are the $350 Gevi Espresso Machine with Grinder and the $350 Casabrews Marenza. While this machine is a seriously budget option, the low, low pricing does raise questions about longevity — which I’ll get into later.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder is a cheap coffee machine, and it feels like it. The scoop is flimsy plastic, and the dosing collar isn’t wide enough to allow the tamper to pass through. The tamper itself is lovely and weighty, though.

There’s no milk jug, which isn’t unprecedented, but is still a kick in the teeth. Casabrews also ships its budget machines with no milk jug, but it sells one for $10. Amzchef doesn’t sell a milk jug at all, so you’ll have to buy a separate one from another brand.

On top of that, the steam wand is supposed to have a 360° swivel, but I’d describe it more as 200° grating. Every time I moved the steam wand, the metal grated against the ball joint.

There’s a bright screen with full-color pictures, which also houses the built-in timer and temperature adjustment screen. This screen is the best part of the machine’s design, although I’m not sure it’s enough of a unique selling point to recommend buying it.

Considering the Amzchef Espresso Machine has a built-in grinder, I was extremely concerned when I unboxed two pressurized portafilter baskets. If you don’t know the difference between pressurized and non-pressurized baskets, I’ll give you a quick rundown. Pressurized portafilter baskets use two walls to force the espresso through a little hole, which creates fluffier crema but destroys delicate flavors. You should use pressurized portafilter baskets if you have pre-ground coffee or an inferior grinder (subtle foreshadowing).

Non-pressurized portafilter baskets have a mesh-like bottom, which allows the espresso to extract naturally, with no extra pressure — that all comes from the fineness of the grind. These baskets are a little trickier to use for beginners, but brew delicate, nuanced espresso if you have a good grinder and good beans.

So I was immediately suspicious when I saw the pressurized baskets. If I’m using a machine with a built-in grinder — ergo, freshly ground coffee — surely I should be provided non-pressurized baskets? A dual-walled basket will over-pressurize my espresso and mask delicate flavors.

Anyway, I had to use what Amzchef provided, so I, of course, tested it with said pressurized baskets.

By default, the grinder grinds for 7 seconds. This resulted in 17.3g of coffee during my tests, but obviously this will change if you grind finer or coarser for different beans. I set the grinder to click 5, as this pulled the ideal 1:2 ratio in 25-28 seconds.

Then, the machine automatically doses water. It pulled 35g of coffee in 28 seconds, which is almost the perfect 1:2 ratio in 25-28 seconds.

Here’s a photo of said default shot. This is with zero customizations — straight from the machine’s brain.

The crema is a little flat, and there’s not a whole lot of depth to the shot. I usually love watching the black ‘body’ of the shot rise up after extraction, but that wasn’t the case with this espresso. It brewed this dark amber color and this dark amber color it remained. As for the taste, it was a little bitter, not particularly strong or weak, but it got the job done. If you’re a total beginner, this would be good enough, but coffee enthusiasts would be better off elsewhere.

However, coffee enthusiasts might be the intended target audience here. There are a few premium, coffee snob-certified features on the Amzchef. You’ve got a PID controller, which controls water temperature, and you can customize temps to your liking. It can go from 190°-201°F, more versatile than Breville’s set-at-200°F PID controller, which you’d find on the $299 Breville Bambino or the $499 Breville Bambino Plus.

All of these features are excellent — I wouldn’t buy an espresso machine without — and resulted in decent espresso. Pressurized portafilters aside, this coffee sits firmly in the “good enough” category. Especially for $229, which is crazy cheap.

I have never seen a bean-to-cup semi-automatic espresso machine cheaper than the Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder. I’ve tested $350 models — the aforementioned Casabrews Marenza and Gevi Espresso Machine with Grinder — but $229? That’s crazy cheap.

The grinder itself has 44 settings, so you can grind from superfine to cold-brew-coarse. As mentioned earlier, the grinder grinds for 7 seconds by default, which you can adjust. To test uniformity, I used my Kruve Coffee Sieves ($189). As espresso grounds should be 300-400 microns, I sift ground coffee through the 500-micron sieve. I’m looking for 100% pass-through. I used click 5 to test espresso, which extracted a 1:2 ratio in 28 seconds.

Here’s a photo to exemplify what I mean. The left is coffee bigger than 500 microns, and the right is coffee smaller than 500 microns (espresso size).

As you can see, this is a non-uniform, inconsistent grinder… and now I know why Amzchef only provides you dual-walled portafilters.

The steam wand is one of the biggest let-dows of the whole machine. It’s weak, spluttery, and takes over sixty seconds to steam a jug of milk (for one coffee).

To activate the steam wand itself, you have to press the steam graphic on the screen, not twist the knob on the side. After pressing the graphic, and the machine reading 107 (temperature), then you twist the knob. It needs a few seconds to switch to steam.

However, the steam wand is really disappointing. I still managed to get half-decent latte art, but the actual texture of the milk was undesirable. It had a layer of foam on top and then wet milk — no velvety aeration throughout.

As you can see, the latte art is still good. But this is after years of practice. I don’t think this is a good machine for beginners to learn on, because you have to know how to tease out “good” milk texture from a sub-par wand.

I don’t really have anything positive to say about the steam wand. If you aren’t fussed about milk drinks, this might be something you can overlook, but for me, I live for decadent, velvety milk, so it’d be a pass.

As it’s just 13 inches wide and 13 inches deep, the Amzchef Espresso Machine is relatively compact, especially for a bean-to-cup machine. If you’re seriously short on space (and budget), I might recommend the Amzchef, but that’s a might.

The machine has an “aluminum alloy” boiler, which means it’s more susceptible to corrosion than a stainless steel boiler, however, there’s no water filter slot in the water tank. Either the machine won’t last as long as a stainless steel boiler, or you’ll need to be seriously on top of descaling — even if you live in a soft water area. There are also no cleaning discs or a cleaning portafilter basket cover for backflushing, unlike Breville and De’Longhi’s machines.

Amzchef advertizes a 2-year warranty if you purchase from the Amzchef website, but the espresso machine is $70 more expensive on the Amzchef site (at time of writing — Amzchef has told me it will correct this). If you register it, the warranty increases to three years. However, you have to spend an extra $70 buying it directly from Amzchef. On the Amzchef warranty page, it reads, “Buy from Amazon, Walmart, or other online retailers? You may get an up-to-2-year limited warranty.” Schrödinger’s warranty!

Amzchef’s representative confirmed that you receive a 2-year warranty regardless of retailer, which is great news, but the language is still too opaque. What if you didn’t have a direct link to the company to find out this information (as I assume most of you won’t)? The language needs to be clearer.

Opaque business practices like this make me incredibly wary about recommending a product. It’s disingenuous. I wouldn’t spend my hard-earned money at a company with obfuscated warranty rules.

Everything about the Amzchef Espresso Machine feels too good to be true. A PID controller, customizable brew temperature, built-in grinder, cold brew, and 360° swivel steam wand for $229? There’s something not quite right here — and you can feel it in the build quality. The water tank is flimsy, the grinder hopper is flimsy, the portafilter is flimsy, and the steam wand grates as it moves. Not only that, but the steam wand is relatively weak, and the low-quality grinder makes for mediocre espresso.

This is a tricky one, because $229 is incredibly cheap for an espresso machine with a grinder. Normally, you’d be expecting to pay $229 for the espresso machine alone and an extra $229 for the grinder — and that would be cheap.

However, I can’t recommend this machine due to its low-quality build, low-quality accessories, and low-quality grinder. I would recommend grabbing the $350 Casabrews Marenza instead (but that’s also incredibly flimsy), or save up more for the Breville Barista Express — often around $499 during sales events like Black Friday — or the De’Longhi Arte Evo — also around $450 during sales events.

#3230. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3229. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Mehta also said that Chevron sees power as a growth opportunity and is using its U.S. natural gas portfolio, key equipment and partnerships to meet rising demand. Notably, Chevron recently signed a 20-year power purchase deal with Microsoft (MSFT) to supply 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter capacity. This project, called Kilby, is expected to see its first power delivery in 2028 and generate mid-teens returns and long-term cash flows.

Mehta ranks No. 536 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.3%. See Chevron Statistics on TipRanks.

Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said.

Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%.

Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47. The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

"Layering in the benefits from the proposed corporate simplification, a multiple well below historical levels and an attractive yield, we believe BIP offers a compelling risk/reward and it remains a preferred idea," said Dodge.

With more organic growth projects in the pipeline and new partnership investment opportunities, Dodge believes that BIP has clearer visibility into where it will deploy capital. That should support continued double-digit growth in funds from operations (FFO) per unit.

Dodge said the semiconductor foundries that BIP is developing with Intel (INTC) are expected to be fully commissioned by the end of 2026, with returns improving through Q4 2026. Dodge expects the joint venture to boost FFO by 300-400 basis points.

Dodge ranks No. 476 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 68% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.5%. See Brookfield Infrastructure Partners KPIs on TipRanks.

#3228. GridAI to buy Wyoming gas firm Pronghorn to power AI data centres

The small Nasdaq company wants to turn gas fields into power for AI, starting with 300 MW in 2027.

GridAI Technologies has agreed to buy Wyoming natural gas producer Pronghorn Resources in an all-stock deal. It plans to build gas-fired power plants for AI data centres, aiming for 300 MW in 2027, but has no named customers yet.

GridAI Technologies has agreed to buy Pronghorn Resources, a natural gas producer in Wyoming, to power AI data centres, the company announced on Thursday. It aims to deliver its first 300 MW of power in 2027.

Pronghorn produces nearly 100 million cubic feet of gas a day from about 3,200 wells in the Powder River Basin. It also owns more than 450 miles of pipelines and has rights to nearly 1 million acres of land and minerals.

GridAI plans to build gas-fired power plants that feed data centres directly, so customers do not have to wait years for a grid connection. It says Pronghorn’s current gas could fuel about 600 MW of power, but that is an estimate. The plants still need to be built and paid for.

The deal is paid in shares, not cash. Pronghorn’s owners will get about 1.25 million GridAI shares plus preferred stock, and the deal is expected to close by 22 November. GridAI, which trades on Nasdaq, was worth about $31M in October, according to StockAnalysis.

GridAI is also taking Wyoming rights to a planned small nuclear reactor design, though it says gas remains its focus for now. It has not named any customers. Last week, Crusoe gave up its Wyoming site to Google, reportedly after failing to find enough customers.

Wyoming is drawing AI investment as other places push back. Google plans a $17B data centre there that will run mainly on gas. Meanwhile, US voters rejected data centres in 40 of 41 local ballot measures this month, as AI fuels a gas-plant boom.

#3227. President Trump calls on Tim Cook to be next NVIDIA CEO

Jensen Huang is out as CEO of NVIDIA after reported love affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a high-ranking executive at the company. Naturally, the American President has called on former Apple CEO Tim Cook to take over as chief executive officer of NVIDIA.

In a post on Truth Social today, President Trump declared that “there is only one man to take his place,” nominating, in spirit, Tim Cook to replace Jensen Huang.

Trump describes the proposed scenario as a legend replacing a legend:

NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! President DONALD J. TRUMP

In reality, that’s probably as far as the Tim Cook/NVIDIA wish casting will go. Cook is enjoying a post-CEO run at Apple as executive chairman of the board.

Part of his responsibilities in the high-paying role include interfacing with world leaders like Trump — even when they suggest he re-enter the CEO workforce.

Anyway, the contrast between Apple’s “textbook” CEO transition and NVIDIA’s disaster version caused by Jensen Huang’s repeated infidelity is on full display.

#3226. Apple Notes adds a powerful new advantage in iOS 27.3

There’s no shortage of note-taking apps on the App Store, but Apple Notes has long been my favorite, and in iOS 27.3 it’s gaining a new advantage: extensive app controls via Siri AI.

Voice-driven computing is on the rise, with AI assistants—including Siri AI—now more capable and intelligent than ever.

Siri AI is already a big upgrade over the old Siri, but it’s getting even better in iOS 27.3.

As we reported last week, iOS 27.3 gives Siri AI many new capabilities across built-in Apple apps on your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more.

The one I’ve been testing the most is Apple Notes. Siri has offered basic Notes-related functionality for years, but it gains a whole new set of powers with the new update.

Here’s everything Siri told me it can do in Notes as of iOS 27.3:

That’s a lot of capabilities that can all now be handled by Siri.

I have nearly 3,000 notes saved in Apple Notes and use the app every day, so it’s been fun seeing what Siri can now do for me. One common example is that I’ve been able to have Siri save a link to the webpage I’m currently viewing inside a note, and even specify exactly where in the note I want it to go.

In theory, third-party notes apps may be able to offer similar controls sometime next year when app skills officially launch. For now though, anyone who wants to control their notes app by voice—or via Spotlight, as I tend to do on my iPad Pro—have another reason to use Apple Notes.

#3225. Google’s Gemini can now read your Google Wallet to help you budget

Users can link bank and card accounts too, but Google may train AI on summaries of their transactions.

Google Wallet joins Gmail, Photos, YouTube and Search as an app Gemini can connect to through Personal Intelligence.

Google is rolling out a Google Wallet connection to all Gemini app users in the US. Gemini can analyse spending, find subscriptions and suggest budgets, with read-only access. Google says it may train AI on summaries of that data if users keep activity on.

Google is letting every Gemini app user in the US connect Google Wallet, so the chatbot can answer questions about their spending, the company announced on Thursday. Users can also link bank and credit card accounts through Plaid for more detailed answers.

After tagging @Google Wallet in a chat, users can ask Gemini to chart last quarter’s spending or help them save $1,000. It can also find subscriptions that went up in price, or use last year’s spending to suggest a holiday budget.

The connection is opt-in and read-only. Gemini can see account data but cannot move, manage or invest money, and users can switch it off at any time. That differs from Google’s Universal Cart, which already lets Gemini take payments.

Google says it does not train its AI directly on Wallet data. But its help pages say that if users keep their Gemini activity on, it may train on summaries of their transactions. Some of those chats may also be read by human reviewers.

Google also launched Memory Summary, a page showing what Gemini remembers about a user, such as their goals and preferences. Users can edit or delete those details. It is not available in Europe or the UK.

#3223. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

#3221. Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence

After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”

Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:

“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”

Google says Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

This was a nice surprise when I opened the app an hour or two ago. It seems to be noticeably better, too.

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

#3220. Cornelis launches CN6000 800G networking to rival Nvidia InfiniBand

Its new 800G network cards aim to stop costly AI chips from sitting idle while they wait for data.

Cornelis’s CN6000 network card and switch, which partner systems will use from early 2027.

Cornelis, which Intel spun out in 2020, has launched CN6000, a family of 800G network cards and switches for AI and supercomputers. It claims lower latency than Nvidia’s InfiniBand, based on its own tests. Partner systems arrive in early 2027.

Cornelis, a networking company spun out of Intel, has launched CN6000, a family of 800G network cards and switches for AI clusters and supercomputers, it announced this week. It is pitching them as a rival to Nvidia’s InfiniBand.

In large AI systems, thousands of chips must constantly swap data. If the network is slow, expensive chips sit idle. “Every minute an accelerator waits on the network is capacity our customers paid for and didn’t use,” said CEO Lisa Spelman.

The main card uses Omni-Path, a networking technology Intel dropped in 2019 before spinning the business off as Cornelis in 2020. Cornelis says the card can handle 1.6 billion messages a second. It also says it is 21% faster than Nvidia’s InfiniBand at passing a small message, though that comes from its own tests.

A faster single message does not mean jobs finish 21% sooner, since that depends on the workload. Cornelis also launched a card for standard Ethernet networks, which most AI data centres use, with support for the newer Ultra Ethernet standard due later.

The cards work with chips from AMD, Intel, Nvidia and Qualcomm. Dell, Lenovo and Supermicro are among the server makers planning to support them, with systems due in early 2027.

Networking has become a hot spot in AI. Nvidia has spent billions on optical links, Huawei is betting on wiring over chips, and startups such as Upscale AI are building ways to connect rival chips. AMD, a Cornelis partner, is also building rack-scale systems to compete with Nvidia.

#3219. IEEE Program Schools Preuniversity Educators On Tech Topics

The TryEngineering workshops help teachers deliver engaging STEM lessons

An educator constructs a microchip model during the IEEE Making a Microchip lesson plan demonstration.

Now in their third year, the IEEE TryEngineering educator sessions continue to empower preuniversity teachers with specialized professional development programs on engineering topics and classroom-tested lessons.

This year’s sessions, held across the United States, have focused on educating teachers about artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. One session was held in Egypt.

In all, 54 educators learned about the engineering design process this year. They received an overview of TryEngineering resources including the Making of a Microchip and Train Your Tree lesson plans.

Workshops are scheduled this year in Greece and Guatemala.

The TryEngineering program is administered by IEEE Educational Activities.

These teachers and guest speakers attended the two-day session held at the Florida Semiconductor Institute and SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.IEEE Educational Activities

Central to the educator session program’s success is its university network. Host campuses welcome teachers into their facilities, where faculty provide background information about some of the technologies being taught, as well as possible engineering career paths and job opportunities for students.

This year’s sessions involved the educators in hands-on projects. Facilitators at each location were selected based on their experience in engineering education, and they worked with the TryEngineering staff on their presentations.

Sixteen teachers from nine schools participated in the session, held in Cairo. It was facilitated by Marwa Soudi, an IEEE member, and Senior Member Stamatis Dragoumanos. Both are past chairs of the IEEE preuniversity coordinating committee. GEMS provided outstanding STEM facilities for teachers, Saudi and Dragoumanos said. Participants received an overview of the Working With Wind Energy and Tall Tower Challenge lesson plans.

Another educator session is scheduled for later this year.

Educators from across the state gathered at the university’s Florida Semiconductor Institute, headquartered in Gainesville, and FSI’s NeoCity high-tech manufacturing campus near Orlando. The session was hosted by Roseanne Perez, an FSI workforce development program specialist, and Sophia Watson, FSI’s assistant director of workforce development. The two-day experience featured an inside look at microelectronics through a guided tour of a SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.

Engineering instructor Mary Acken facilitated hands-on lesson demonstrations for the 15 attending teachers.

Reflecting on the workshop’s impact, one participant said the SkyWater tour was excellent, the instructors were great, and the teachers enjoyed learning from like-minded educators.

Michael Kozicki, an IEEE member, and Stefan Myhajlenko from the university’s engineering school welcomed 11 Arizona teachers to the Tempe campus.

The session was facilitated by Janet Hartkopf, an Arizona school leader and a former TryEngineering educator session participant. Hartkopf highlighted collaborative learning, the need for diverse perspectives in engineering education, and career paths.

The teachers received instruction on how to implement the hands-on lessons in their classrooms, and they toured the university’s NanoFab facility to observe microelectronics research.

“This training was amazing!” said a participant who leads an elementary after-school STEM club. “I loved the hands-on lessons and e-books, which I will definitely be using with my students. I am excited to explore all the resources on the TryEngineering website. The experts from ASU were great.”

Sixteen STEM educators attended this session, held at the university’s International Institute for Biosensing in Minneapolis. Its director, Patricia Khashayar, an IEEE member, introduced participants to the capabilities of the university’s Supercomputing Institute and Nano Center.

Under the guidance of Claire Dietz, an education and outreach coordinator, and Pam Schumacher, an instructor at St. Paul College, the teachers completed classroom-ready lessons including a photonics experiment using the Nano Center’s equipment. Schumacher attended last year’s TryEngineering educator session.

Nano Center Director Sarah Swisher, an IEEE senior member, provided an overview of semiconductor operations and highlighted growing job opportunities for the state’s young people.

The experience inspired all 16 teachers to plan student field trips to the Nano Center during the upcoming academic year, they said.

“Great class!” one participant said. “I’m excited to bring some of the TryEngineering materials back to our school.”

This year’s sessions built on the momentum from last year when, with financial support from Onsemi’s Giving Now program, nearly 80 teachers attended sessions across five U.S. states and Mexico.

Driven by that success and the demand for more, the IEEE Educational Activities Board continued its support. Upcoming global sessions are expected to expand the program’s international footprint.

“I appreciated the time to collaborate with peers on how to implement hands-on lessons,” one participating teacher this year said. Some participants said they planned follow-up visits with the experts and campus tours.

You can learn more about the sessions by emailing TryEngineering.

Debra Gulick is director of IEEE student and academic educational programs.

#3217. Alexander Rinke says Europe needs AI champions to share in the next wave of AI value

Alexander Rinke told the TNW Podcast that companies and public agencies want to own their AI weights. The Celonis co-founder and co-CEO also set out his test for real product-market fit.

TNW’s Cristian Dina (left) and Celonis co-CEO Alexander Rinke at HumanX in Amsterdam, 23 September 2026

Thirty years ago, Europe’s GDP was roughly on par with the US, Alexander Rinke told TNW. Today it is dramatically less. The Celonis co-founder and co-CEO does not want AI to make that gap wider.

Rinke spoke to Cristian Dina for the TNW Podcast at HumanX in Amsterdam on 23 September. Earlier that day he had joined a panel on stage called “Can Europe Actually Build Sovereign AI?”. Earlier guests include Steve Lucas of Boomi, Arvind Jain of Glean, and Daniel Dines of UiPath. The full conversation is in the video below.

Countries and groups of countries such as Europe want control over parts of the AI stack, Rinke said. They want to know where their data and their IP go. Europe also needs its own companies to take part in an AI economy that will be huge.

“We need to really foster local champions, not because we don’t trust the Americans or we think AI is going to kill us all. Just because we want to make sure we take part of the upside.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

Celonis is one example, he said. Its headquarters are in New York and Munich, and it has more than 20 offices around the world, with a strong presence in Germany, Spain and the UK. Europe is “not a satellite for us,” he said.

For a company or a public agency, sovereign AI means owning its own AI, Rinke said. In the end, that means owning the model weights.

“They don’t want to give all of their data to any model to train on that data.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

Every organisation is like a snowflake, he said, so its processes and their context are unique. That needs open platforms that can be installed in sovereign environments. Celonis keeps a customer’s process data with the customer and does not send it anywhere. It also helps customers tune open-source models for specific business tasks. For those tasks, he said, they can get the same or better results than with frontier models.

Rinke started Celonis 15 years ago with his co-founders, Martin Klenk and Bastian Nominacher. They first wanted to build models that could simulate how a business works. To feed a simulation, they needed to know how the business ran today, and companies could not tell them.

“So we built an x-ray machine that looks at the data the business generates and x-rays how the processes work.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

Celonis now calls this process intelligence. It maps how work really gets done, across systems and outside them, so companies can redesign it with AI. The company has about 3,500 people, he said.

Celonis recently bought Ikigai Labs, an MIT spin-off. Ikigai builds specialised models for tabular and time-series data and for what-if simulation. A large language model can use them as a tool, Rinke said, for jobs such as forecasting a supply chain or deciding whether to settle an insurance claim.

Asked about an IPO or new funding, Rinke spoke about the next phase of growth instead. He pointed to the Context Model that Celonis launched and to the Ikigai deal. Celonis describes the Context Model as a living model of a business in motion, built from its operational data and connected to its strategy.

Many startup pitches claim product-market fit that the company does not have, Rinke said. His test has four questions. Is the product valuable? Is it uniquely valuable, or easy to replace? Is it repeatable, or custom each time? Will customers keep paying for it?

“It’s easy to say that you have. It’s very easy to put on a slide for VCs.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

If the answer to all four is yes, the next step is what he calls product-market-people fit: the organisation needed to scale it. Scaling too early can grow revenue that does not last, he said, especially in a boom market like AI.

Celonis was his first real venture. The founders started it during their studies, and Rinke put his master’s on hold and never finished it. They bootstrapped for five years, and winning the first enterprise clients without references was very hard, he said.

Venture capital is a good idea if a company wants to move quickly, Rinke said. But it does not replace the work a bootstrapped company has to do.

“You shouldn’t build the company to raise capital. You should build the company for customers.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

He now works much more closely with Celonis engineers than he did a few years ago. He oversees some technical projects himself and is involved in how the company adopts AI internally. Asked whether he is technical, he said: “Yeah, pretty technical.”
