#3195. Inter (INTR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

AI now resolves about 85% of client requests, and credit card growth is set to resume soon.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Inter & Co, Inc. (INTR +4.67%) reported its 14th consecutive quarter of profit growth, attributed by management to its BanTech model that integrates banking services with a scalable technology architecture. The company reported a significant strategic focus on artificial intelligence, including the deployment of over 700 internal models and a new strategic partnership with SpaceXAI. Leadership changes were implemented during the quarter to align organizational structure with objectives for growth, monetization, and operational excellence. Management stated that the credit portfolio expansion currently emphasizes secured lending products, such as mortgages and private payroll loans, to navigate a challenging macroeconomic environment. Profitability remains a priority, with the company maintaining an efficiency ratio near 42% while continuing to grow its active client base.

Rafa Vitória: Hi, everyone. I'm Rafa Vitória, IR Officer at Inter, and I would like to welcome you to Inter's third. Available in Portuguese. To access it, press the globe icon on the lower right side of your Zoom screen, then select the Portuguese room. Please be advised that all participants will be in listen-only mode and that the conference is being recorded. You may submit online questions at any time today using the Q&A box on the webcast. A replay will be available at the company's IR website. Here with me today is João Vitor Menin, our CEO, Alexandre Riccio, our COO, Francisco Santos, our CGO, and Santiago Stel, our CFO. João will start sharing the strategic overview.

João Vitor Menin: Thank you very much, Rafa. Good morning, everyone. Thanks for joining us again to discuss our third quarter results. First of all, before we go into any page, I want to leave you with one important message. I have great confidence in the model we have been building at Inter for a while. I call it the BanTech model, and it works. Today, I will share how we built our story and how it gives us the strength to look at the future with excitement. To explain where this confidence comes from, I would like to start at the origin. This is how we introduced Inter to the market back in 2018 when we did our IPO.

I still remember presenting this page on the roadshow and how much it meant to all of us. At the time, the market saw traditional banks trying to become digital and fintechs trying to become a bank and Inter was in the intersection of it. That intersection was never a compromise. It was our conviction, and it is one of our biggest strengths to date. We were born from banking, but also powered by tech. As a licensed bank, we offer the full set of banking products, such as credit, deposits, payments, investments, and insurance. As a tech company, we have speed. We run asset-light, no branch network, distribution at fintech cost.

We call this combination the BanTech model I told you before, and it still holds true today, maybe more than ever. I'm sure you have heard this story before. Why am I bringing it up again today? Because this design is what makes Inter resilient in any environment. We're not stuck in one product or in one specific credit cycle. The BanTech model creates something strong, and it is built for any cycle, for any moment. Let me explore it a bit further. First, our balance sheet fortress. 70% of our loan book is secured, and our cost of funding is consistently lower than our peers, digital and traditional banks.

That gives us resilience when the environment gets tougher and room to keep growing when it gets better. Second, regulation. The regulator is moving towards the book we have already built, secured credit, such as private payroll, real estate, or invoice discount. We are ahead where the market is heading. Third, the competitive landscape. In a crowded market of banks and fintechs, clients keep choosing Inter. We are very proud that today we have 90% of all the Pix transactions in Brazil. Our daily logins just hit a new record this month. We stand out because clients find everything in one place and use it every day.

We call this the strong combination of serving clients with convenience, savings, and trust. The fourth reason is technology. AI is already part of how we run Inter, and we are building on top of strong foundations, especially our data vault. Most importantly, we have the DNA to innovate. If you ask me, "How can Inter innovate so much?" I would answer you, "It's all about being bold." We don't adapt the future, we design it, and we have a track record of doing so. The first digital bank in Brazil back in 2015, the first bank to migrate to cloud in 2017, and also the first super app in the Americas in 2020.

Every time, the same choice, to lead, to disrupt, and every time, we have been building that with the best partners. Today, we are making the same choice with the next technological wave, AI. It is not a plan, it's a red run, and it's a great opportunity for Inter again, and we are already seizing it. Not only we have the better models and more efficiency in our teams, but we are going even further. As I mentioned at our Owners' Day, we have the perfect combination of our data vault, our 3SA approach, and our agentic engine called Seven.

The same way we have launched hundreds of versions of our super app, I'm sure we will launch hundreds of versions of Seven ahead. Our ambition is for Seven to become the core of our client experience, and I'm sure that now we're just scratching the surface. As we did before on the previous technological waves, again, we are now partnering with the best. We just recently connected with SpaceX AI, and they are now our strategic partner for us in the AI world. But AI does not work alone. It's fed by data, and data comes from the relationship with our clients. That is where the magic begins, and that's why our model shines.

The BanTech approach created something bigger, a flywheel of learning effects, now even more empowered by AI. Let me explain how our flywheel works. It starts with the relationship. Customers come to Inter first, and they come most often. The more of their financial life sits with us, the more data we have, and more they trust us. With more data comes intelligence. Every decision and its outcome feed our data vault, and AI turns that data into more personalized experience, better credit models, and faster operations. With that intelligence, our capabilities grow. The client is better served, use more products with us, and brings more data to the vault.

That is what makes each loop larger, and the flywheel restarts. More relationship, more data, more learning, each time faster and larger. When this flywheel runs, Inter captures continuous growth and sustainable profitability. This is not theory. It's already showing up in our numbers. For instance, this quarter, our ARPAC reached its highest level ever. Santi will walk you through it later today. But the message is quite simple. The more the flywheel turns, the more value each client generates, and the more data flows into our data vault. This is what we call the learning effect. But technology alone does not turn the flywheel. People do.

To lead Inter into the future, we are evolving our structure into two clear focuses: growth and operational excellence. We are welcoming Francisco Santos as our Chief Growth Officer. He will be focused on growth and monetization. Francisco will use the flywheel I just described to grow not only our client base, but also our monetization, with our data vault and our learning effects supporting that journey. Xande, who you might know already, steps in as our COO, focused on operational excellence and on improving our credit and collection capabilities. He will turn the intelligence of our data vault and the power of AI into even smarter credit decisions and lighter operations.

Also, Santi continues as our CFO, focused on profitability and capital allocation, turning growth into returns with discipline. Think about this flywheel. Francisco makes every turn bigger, Xande makes every turn run better, and Santi makes sure each turn is profitable. As I said, it's people who turn the flywheel. Together with these leaders, our 4,000 employees do it every day, guided by our strong culture. With the right team and the right culture, I'm sure we will keep building Inter ahead. Now, it's my pleasure to invite Francisco to share a few words with you. He will share his first impressions of Inter. Francisco, welcome, and the floor is yours.

Francisco Santos: Thank you, João. It's a pleasure to be here. Inter has a remarkable journey, and I've admired what this company has built for a long time. I'm finishing my second week at Inter. It's been great to see how customer choose Inter and actively engage with us. We have a customer base that most companies would love to have, and I see a tremendous potential to deepen relationships and increase monetization. Data, cloud, and AI are not side projects here. They are embedded in how the company operates, allowing us to move faster and continuously learn and improve. Above all, I see the team highly motivated to achieve more and willing to do things differently.

So, my initial focus is on those three areas. First, retail banking. We want to enhance primary banking relationships and increase monetization. That means more customer choosing Inter as their main bank and generating more value for each relationship. Second, SMBs. I see significant opportunity here. Business customer already bring their deposits to Inter. The next step is to deepen those relationships through products, leveraging data and technology capabilities that have worked so well in retail. To help lead this effort, we brought Frederico Alves to Inter. He brings over 20 years of experience in payment and banking, having led products and businesses at Itaú and Fiserv. He's a great addition to the team.

Last but not least, looking ahead, I want to bring fresh perspectives and work alongside the team to help shape the next chapter of Inter's growth. I am very grateful for the warm welcome I received, and I am excited to be part of this team. I'm looking forward to work closely with Xande because growth and operational excellence need to go hand in hand. Thanks, Xande, for receiving me. Thanks, João. Xande, over to you.

Alexandre Riccio: Thank you, Francisco. I'm looking forward to working side by side with you. Hello, everyone. I'm very excited about this new chapter at Inter, and it is an honor to lead operations at such an important moment for the company. As João said, my mandate is to turn the intelligence of our data vault and the power of AI into even smarter credit decisions and lighter operations. In other words, excellence in credit underwriting and AI-powered operations at scale. It rests on three focuses. First, credit. We're taking our next-gen foundation models to full scale, moving to one single model per client, so every decision is smarter and more consistent using the data that our client relationships generates. Second, collections.

We want to reach full maturity in collection execution and products, rebuilding our processes with GenAI and automation. Third, operations. We're scaling up the transformation of our processes using agentic AI, automating steps, and simplifying the experience for our clients. João showed that AI is already running at Inter. Our job is to take it to the core of our operations. The logic is the same in all three. Use technology to remove what does not add value and give our teams time for what does. That makes us more efficient, and efficiency is what turns operational excellence into financial results, lower cost to serve, better credit decisions, and more profitable growth.

As Francisco said, growth and operational excellence have to move together, and you see this in the numbers. With that, I will hand it over to Santi, who will take you through our financial performance of the quarter. Thank you.

Santiago Stel: Good morning, everyone. A public welcome here to Francisco. Really great to have you in the team. Xande, it is great to have you focused on credit underwriting and operational excellence, as they are key drivers to execute our ambitions. Now, let me walk you through the financial performance of the quarter. Starting on revenue, on a net basis, we reached BRL 2.7 billion, up 26% year-on-year, and up 3% quarter-on-quarter. This is a run rate net revenue of BRL 10.9 billion, or gross of nearly BRL 20 billion, a very substantial figure that shows the materiality of our performance. Net interest income was BRL 2.1 billion, up 30% year-on-year, representing 78% of our revenue.

Fee income was BRL 611 million, up 13%, in line with the growth of our active client base. What matters is that these results show that our flywheel is working very well. Each quarter, we have a larger client base, a fast-growing loan portfolio, and a strong set of products and services to complement our revenue base. Now, let me show you how this looks on a per-client basis. We reached 46.8 million total clients, up 13% year-on-year, with more than 27 million of them being active. On monetization of these clients, we are making great progress quarter after quarter. Our gross ARPAC reached BRL 59.7 per month, up 5% year-on-year, establishing a new record.

Net ARPAC after the deduction of interest expense was BRL 35.6, up 7%, also a new record. Growing revenue higher than client growth is a key component of our strategy, especially considering the sizable existing client base we have already established. On the cost side, our cost to serve was BRL 13.3 per client per month, a flattish figure when you look at the prior quarters. This gap between ARPAC and cost to serve is our margin per active client, which reached BRL 22.3 per month, establishing another quarter of record. Two factors are behind this performance. The first, deeper engagement and higher credit penetration as our flywheel gets faster, bigger, and better, as João mentioned earlier.

The second, our newer cohorts are starting stronger. They begin with an ARPAC that is BRL 10 greater than the one of the prior quarters. This is how client growth turns into returns, and it is in the NIM where we can see this. Our NIM 2.0 reached 9.96% this quarter, staying very close to the 10% landmark figure. Let me walk you through two key points that play in this quarter. The first, we are 70 basis points higher year-on-year, with an average of 15 basis points greater on a quarter-on-quarter basis. This despite the increase in our leverage. So on a same capital structure basis, the NIM improvement is even stronger.

Second, as we anticipated in our last earnings call, this quarter was marked by lower inflation, which impacted NII. If we were to normalize for the inflation effect, we also grew 10 to 15 basis points per quarter on average since the fourth quarter of 2025. That reflects the evolution of mix and pricing, with cards reshaping and private payroll being the main drivers. All of this to say, the roughly 40 basis points of NIM expansion that we expected to have in this calendar year 2026 is very well on track, and we expect to close the year with a NIM at around 10%, as we have been mentioning.

On a risk-adjusted basis, we improved 12 basis points year-on-year, despite the evolution of cost of risk. This margin expansion is built upon an ROE-driven credit strategy that we have been executing thoroughly year after year. Our expanded loan portfolio reached BRL 58.1 billion, up 25% year-on-year, and up 5% quarter-on-quarter. Our strategy here is clear, a credit mix that is sustainable for the client across the cycle, making it a real win-win value proposition. Today, around 70% of the book has some type of guarantee, and this matters especially in this current environment with high household leverage and high interest rates. Our growth is driven by these type of products, with mortgages and private payroll being the main ones.

Real estate loans reached BRL 19.9 billion, up 37% year-on-year, and is now the largest portfolio of product in our mix, representing 34% of the total. This is where expertise shows the most, the best experience and the least bureaucracy in the market to get these loans. That means an efficient operation, low delinquency, and a very profitable product. On private payroll, we reached BRL 3.1 billion, 2.5 times greater than what we had a year ago. I will cover private payroll in depth in a following page. On cards, we grew 18% as we deliberately reshaped the book towards installments with interest income, which is now 37% up.

Personal loans are almost flat, with FGTS running off, and our cautious approach on unsecured credit lines such as buy now, pay later, and overdraft. Overall, we are growing well above the credit market in Brazil, which is growing on a high single-digit basis. We are managing credit cycle with discipline. Let me take you through this page with care, starting with NPL and then NPL and stage 3 formations. NPL over 90 days reached 5.3% on the expanded portfolio, up 29 basis points. The increase came mainly from our portfolio mix into products that I will cover on dedicated pages right after this one. The Desenrola also had an effect of 14 basis points in this KPI.

NPL from 90 to 15 days, which measures the short-term delinquency, decreased to 4.2% from 4.5% in the prior quarter, and is an early sign that delinquency is improving. NPL formation, which is on the bottom left of this page, decreased from 1.83% last quarter to 1.74% this one. This improvement came mainly from private payroll, helped by the automatic relinkage and from credit cards. This is consistent with the early delinquency we just saw. Fewer newer loans are entering delinquency. I will detail later this point. On stage 3 formation, on the bottom right of the page, it was 2.10%, up from 2.12% in the prior quarter, and is impacted by the Desenrola program.

The program started in May, and it targeted credit card debt and unsecured personal loans. Since we do not offer unsecured personal loans, for us, it was the credit card, the one that entered in this program. At the end of September, we had renegotiated a little more than BRL 160 million. This added close to 20 basis points of stage 3 formation because it moved contracts that were fully written off into stage 3. Excluding the program, the stage 3 formation would have been flat at 1.9%, both in second and third quarter.

Now, on the cost of risk and coverage, all-in cost of risk was 5.9% this quarter, pretty much in line with the prior one and consistent with the 6% figure that we have been signaling as our new steady state. As we said, two internal decisions explain most of the increase versus last year, the growth of private payroll, two, the reshaping of credit cards. Excluding private payroll, cost of risk was 5.3%. Coverage ratio, on the other hand, increased slightly from 134% to 135%. Our provisions cover the delinquent balance with a comfortable margin. Here, we added a dedicated page for private payroll, so we can deep dive in it.

One year ago, our loan portfolio of this product was BRL 1.3 billion, and now it is BRL 3.1 billion. Our active clients went from 282,000 to 759,000 clients. As I mentioned, this has been the product that drove delinquency up, but most of the missed payments happen when an employee changes employer, and we have two levers to solve this. The first, the automatic relinkage. Around 30% of the delinquent balance has already been relinked, so we can follow the client to the new employer and keep collecting. Second, the private payroll insurance with about 40% penetration. The effect is showing in asset quality.

NPL formation in private payroll fell to 3.2% in the quarter from 4.9% in the prior one. Stage 3 formation was 5.8%, up from 4.8%, because our stage transfer policy keeps loans under observation before they move across stages. It does not mean new delinquency, and NPL formation confirms that. On the right-hand side, you can see the J-curve of this product with a break-even on month three and then a positive return profile. Now moving on to funding. Our total funding reached BRL 81 billion, up 19% year-on-year and 5% quarter-on-quarter. It is a high-growth and diversified funding franchise. Demand deposits reached BRL 20.7 billion, up 13% year-on-year. Time deposits reached BRL 37 billion, up 20% year-on-year.

Securities issued reached BRL 17.8 billion, up 45%, as we keep diversifying our sources beyond just deposits. Deposits per active client, a key metric, reached BRL 2.1 billion, a new high, up 3% year-on-year. Our loans-to-deposit ratio is 69%, up from 65% a year ago, which means that we are putting our excess liquidity to work in the credit book. Let me show you how this follows in terms of funding costs. Our cost of funding, as we have mentioned many times, is one of our greatest competitive advantages. This quarter, we reached 70% of CDI. There were two factors playing out. The first one was seasonality.

As you can see in the chart, the third quarter goes up because the number of business days, 65% this quarter, is higher than the 61% in the second quarter. Normalized by business days, our cost of funding would have been 68%, in line with the prior quarters. The second factor is Selic, and therefore the mix of our deposits. With the Selic still high, our deposit mix are trending towards higher-yielding deposits, pushing the funding cost high. That explains most of the difference versus last year. As we have said many times, our cost of funding remains one of our key competitive advantages.

We have kept expenses controlled while we keep scaling the business, and this is one of the advantages of the digital banking model that we have built. Total expenses, which little over BRL 1 billion, up 3% quarter-on-quarter. There are a few drivers of this performance. The first, administrative expenses, which grew 2% this quarter, or 17% on a yearly basis, driven by branding and technology costs. Other lines benefited from scale, which balanced the overall evolution. Second was personnel expenses, which grew 4% in the quarter and only 10% in the year, with average headcount staying roughly flat.

Third, depreciation and amortization, which grew 6% in the quarter and 38% in the year because of the amortization of prior investments in technology infrastructure and our super app. Looking ahead, we expect a fourth quarter with seasonally higher expenses, but a 2027 with an important gain in operational leverage as we collect the benefits of our business model. Jumping to operational leverage, our efficiency ratio reached 41.9%, more than 3 percentage points better than a year ago. Since first quarter of 2023, our revenue has grown 2.7 times, while personal administrative expenses grew 1.8 times. This is operational leverage in action. In three and a half years, our efficiency ratio went from 62% to 42%.

The pace over the quarter was smaller, 15 basis points, because revenue growth was more moderated, in part because of the inflation impact that I commented before. The direction is clear, and there is still room to improve as we collect more benefits from the new investments. Jumping into profitability, this page, as we mentioned many times, gets us very proud. We delivered the 14th consecutive quarter of net income growth, 14th consecutive quarter of net income growth, reaching BRL 425 million this quarter, up 26% relative to the BRL 336 million of the third quarter of last year. Annualized ROE reached 15.8%, up 160 basis points relative to a year ago.

This quarter was marginally more timid than the prior one because of inflation and also because the average equity, meaning the denominator in the ROE formula, increased due to the positive mark-to-market in securities. Overall, this page shows a clear trend that makes us very proud, and we expect to continue delivering. When we compare our profitability in the context of the banking industry, we can see that on an ROE and an ROA basis. On the top, on ROE, we are the 12th in the ranking when we look at the first semester of the banking industry.

More importantly, on ROA, which adjusts for the capital structure that is very different across banks, we are in the top third of the industry. When we factor the fact that we are growing and investing heavily, being the top third of the industry is something that makes us very proud, considering the size that we have, which is still a lot lower than what we expect as we continue being a disruptor and a fast-growth player in the industry. Last quarter, we mentioned that we were capital neutral. What we can see in this quarter is an even stronger pattern.

Our CT1 ratio reached 12.2% at Banco Inter level, up 70 basis points from the 11.5% that we had in the prior quarter. Banco Inter profits generated 100 basis points of capital, and the growth in credit and operational risk consumed 70 basis points. So the operational result added 30 net basis points of capital, while our loan portfolio grew 5% this quarter. As we can see in the middle chart, we have significant excess capital ready to be deployed in our business. This is a result of our corporate structure that is highly efficient. With that said, I will pass it back to João for his closing remarks. Thank you.

João Vitor Menin: Thank you, Santi, Francisco, and Xande. Hearing your perspectives on Inter and also the opportunities ahead and how the results were on this quarter makes me even more excited about our future. Now, I would like to go back to what matters most from this quarter. Here are four takeaways that I would like to reinforce. First, credit growth. We grew our expanded credit portfolio 25%, almost 3x the market. That was driven by our strongest products, real estate, private payroll, and cards. That is the BanTech in credit, banking products with the power of technology. Second, asset quality. Our cost of risk is at 5.9%, flat versus the last quarter, even with the market deteriorating further.

This is the balance sheet we built for any cycle, with 70% of our book secured. It is not luck, it is design. Third, our NIMs. We are around 10%, 70 basis points above a year ago, even with the impact of IPCA. This is our data vault empowered by AI, turning into even smarter pricing and better credit decisions. Last, efficiency. Our efficiency ratio this quarter hit 41.9%, 322 basis points better than last year, with operating leverage in action. So, growth, asset quality, margins, and efficiency, all moving together. This is a flywheel in motion and a model built for any cycle. I am sure that the best for Inter is yet to come. Thank you very much.

Rafa Vitória: Now we open the Q&A session. Our first question is from Fernanda Sayão from JPMorgan. Fernanda, your mic is open. Please go ahead.

Fernanda Sayão: Hey, João, Santi, Rafa. Thank you for the opportunity to ask questions. My question is about private payroll. Since the operational improvements went live in September, how are newer cohorts behaving compared to older ones? Also, how is the cost of risk trending at the margin? Just the last one, if you could also comment on the impacts you are seeing from the bundled insurance. Thank you.

Alexandre Riccio: Hi, Fernanda. This is Xande speaking. Thank you for your question. I will take a step back on the private payroll loans, and the first point is about the excitement with the product. We remain excited with the future prospects for the product, the profitability, and see it as strategic for Inter, aligned with our distribution channels. This is a first message. As far as the processes goes, we know and we have been saying in the earnings calls since last year that it would be a journey, and it has been a journey. Maybe a little bit slower than what everybody initially imagined.

But in the last quarter, reality is that we did have a material improvement with the automatic relinkage. Having said that, I would say that we have three very important things that happened with the product in this last quarter. The first one, again, is relinkage. The relinkage helped us both on NPLs and on cost of risk, roughly 2% improvements on NPLs and 1% improvement in cost of risk. As we move along, we are going to see these improvements mature more. That is our expectation. The second point is insurance. As we mentioned in the last call, we were starting to do the insurances.

Now we are at about 40% penetration, and it is also a process that matures as we go, and which links to your question on cohorts. Our expectation is that the newer cohorts are going to start behaving better than the older cohorts, given relinkage and given the fact that we have 40% penetration on insurance. Finally, when we think a third factor that is very important for us is pricing, and the thing about pricing is it leads to the production. The volume of underwriting for us is a lot more an output than an input, so we drive it through ROE, we drive it through observing how the behavior of the delinquency is.

As we make adjustments in pricing, we see sensitivity in underwriting volume, and we have been laser-focused on guaranteeing that we grow at a steady pace. Thank you, Fernanda.

Rafa Vitória: Our next question is from Tito Labarta. Tito, your mic is open. Please go ahead.

Only, let's say, only BRL 60 billion. With that in place, we are comfortable on growing between 20%-25% going forward, which is, I would say, almost 2.5x the market. Again, thinking about the opportunities that we still have on cards, private payroll, mortgage, home equity, and SMEs, I do see that 20%-25% range quite feasible and prudent. Last, it is about team. He might add later about few opportunities that we have. Also, Xande, 100% focused on operational excellence and credit and underwriting capabilities.

With all that in place, Tito, despite of the macro, I see a great chance for Inter to differentiate against our competitors. The message is prudent but excited with the pace of growth ahead.

Tito Labarta: Okay, very helpful, João Vitor. Thank you. Maybe just one follow-up, I guess, by segment, should we expect the secured lending to grow faster? How do you think about unsecured lending in 2027?

João Vitor Menin: Tito, I mean, we have been answering these questions for many, many quarters already. People thought that we were going to grow super-fast on credit card once we, let's say, crack the code on underwriting and collection. The true story is, we still see a lot of opportunities on the secured portfolio. When going back to the size of our portfolio, our market share at Pix is at 9%, but our market share at private payroll, public payroll, SMEs collateralized by receivables, home equity, mortgage is still small in a sense. So I do see a lot of opportunities for us to keep growing strongly on the secured portfolio.

Again, a good opportunity on cards as well, as Xande was mentioning, better collections, better underwriting. That said, overall, pretty much this 7%-ish ratio between secured and unsecured should keep this trend, I'd say, ahead for at least the next, I'd say, one or two years. So that's how I foresee the balance between secured and unsecured ahead.

Tito Labarta: Okay, perfect. Thank you very much, João Vitor.

Is it possible to see higher payout ratio, buyback, or do not believe that we are already in this point of discuss a kind of higher capital distribution?

Santiago Stel: Yeah, good morning. I will take that one here. Santiago speaking. On asset quality, we are very proud of what we are showing this quarter. There are many metrics in the presentation that you can see that it is pointing to an improvement, early delinquency, 15 to 90 day, NPL formation. This is the result of a very strong work that we have been doing on several fronts, and maybe on the most two iconic portfolio, which is credit cards and private payroll, which have been driving NIM growth, but we want to, you know, drive risk-adjusted NIM growth sustainable through time.

That is the consequence of a very active management on those two specific products, because the remaining products have performed very well and stable through the cycle. So those two have added a substantial level of revenues. On the cost side, we have been working through the operational side on private payroll, as Xande mentioned, and on the credit side as well, on UX, on collection, and so on. When we see that, we get to a cost of risk that we reported, 5.9%, same number as per quarter, or actually 3 basis points lower. That is consistent with what we have been signaling, which is at around 6% cost of risk. We have Desenrola playing out also.

That benefited us in the second and third quarter. But going forward, we think that the cost of risk that we have reported, adjusted by the Desenrola impact, is the one that we expect for the coming quarters to continue, which is around 6%. That is very exciting because it allows us to continue to have this positive trend on our margins. Now moving to capital, we have been also working very strongly there on ROE density and optimizing our capital. The ROE going up obviously helps.

The structure that we have with the holding on the top is very efficient, and through the last two, three years, we have been paying JCP or tax on capital to move the excess capital to the holding where it is more profitable. That makes the math of excess capital a bit more complicated, but we try to make it easy in our disclosure. We have BRL 2.1 billion of excess capital up in the holding. When you translate that to how many percentage points would it mean at the bank if we were to move that capital down, it is around 4 percentage points. Therefore, the total number is around 19.5% of total capital consolidated.

What will we do with that excess capital? Our primary role would be to deploy it in the business. That is the reason why we have it. So, we would like to do it obviously with caution, as João mentioned, and then the shareholders will decide the dividend policy as they see fit. But the primary goal of the excess capital is to be deployed in the business to grow it through time.

Thiago Batista: Thanks a lot, Santiago. Very clear.

Alexandre Riccio: Hi, Leduc. This is Xande speaking. Let us go. There are a few steps here to cover when we look at the credit cards. We know that we look at early NPLs and the effects that those have in cost of risk and longer term NPLs. We have been able to drive the portfolio, but reality is that in the short term, we reduced the pace of growth. For that, obviously, we have to observe macro and see what are the reactions. Typically, the end of the year is not the best time to open credit in credit cards. If I was to ask when is time to accelerate, I would look more into the beginning of next year than in the end of this year, in this fourth quarter, given both macro and the cyclical delinquency that we observe every year in this time of the year. Now, I think it's important to highlight also all the focus that we're going to give in credit and collections with the new structure. I'm super excited about the changes that we made.

These are generic models, so they're going to be able to help us improve on collections, help us improve on propensity models for cross-selling, AMLs. There is a lot to come as we move along. Optimizing, something that we're doing. The scaling is what we expect to be able to do more next year.

Pedro Leduc: Very useful, Xande. Thank you.

Gustavo Schroden: All right. Thank you, guys.

João Vitor Menin: Well, Mario, thank you for the question. Maybe I would say it is the best question of the Q&A, to be honest. I like to say that we did a 10x thing for the past 10 years, so from 5,000 clients, 45 million clients, a small company in a few cities in Brazil to 100% of clients in all over Brazil. And that was possible mainly because we were able to tackle all the technology available back then, and we had the right mindset.

So, I know that back then, we had a few banks trying to be more efficient on how they were opening branches, how they were trying to optimize the cost with their own data centers, and Inter did something completely different. I like to say, Mario, I call this cognitive change. Not to think linearly, but how to disrupt the way you have been doing things. We launched the first digital bank in Brazil. 10 years later, 2026, I really see AI, despite all the buzz and all the excitement, but I really see AI as the next technological wave.

I have been working alongside with Guilherme Ximenes, our CTO, to again, to try to disrupt the way Inter are doing our business today. As I told, we have superior position. When we are trying to figure out how to put AI at the center of it, how I run the business, there are three things that is important. We like to say that first people, so how we do this cognitive change around our senior managers, it is what I am working hard on that. The second thing is about the process, how we do Inter more efficient.

This is what I would say that I like to do the most at Inter. So how can we think about the future, bring it faster ahead of the competition? In that sense, we decided to team up, which we believe is the best company available today. We did some research, some interactions, a lot of work on our end, and we believe that xAI is the best for us to put Seven, which is our core engine, to seize this opportunity of AI. To put Seven on the core of it. Actually, we just launched a new version of our website. We launched a website called seven.co, which is focused on that AI center, AI-first approach. We do not have the agreement with them. It is not about profit share, so we are just using them as a strategic vendor.

Also, we are participating in a client advisory board, Guilherme is there, to get the best technology, to be ahead. I mean, I am super excited. The same way cloud computing and the microservice, the App Store, Google Play played this 10x impact at Inter back then, I am kind of convinced and super excited that we have the same opportunity today. I mean, how fast, how impactful it will be to Inter? I do not know. The thing is that I am doing the best I can, and I am putting all my efforts.

That is what I, to be honest, I like to do the most, and that is what I believe are my better skills on connecting the technology to how we serve clients in a different way, different from where the market is headed. A long answer, but that is how I see this partnership. That is how I see this technological wave, and I believe that we are going to disrupt ourselves like we disrupted the incumbent banks back then. So, I think that we're going to have an amazing journey ahead, and in spite of the macro, in spite of everything, some headwinds, I think that the tailwind there, it's super nice.

Mario Pierry: João, just to get a little bit more color, then this partnership, is there like a time, a period, and is there like a revenue sharing, or how does it work?

João Vitor Menin: No, Mario, there is no profit share, as I mentioned. It's just that we elected SpaceX AI as our main partner for developing everything on cloud using Cursor, that is a component now that belongs to the group. How we're going to do the software development life cycle, how we're going to power Seven, which is our core engine thing. As I mentioned, how we put xAI to help on the three Ps, the people, the process, and the product. So that's about having the best, we believe, in the world available to support Inter going forward.

So, no partnerships in terms of revenue, but just being able to access first with this client advisory board that I mentioned, and Guilherme is super on top of it, to again, disrupt ourselves, so we avoid that someone else will disrupt Inter as we did 10 years ago. That's pretty much the vision behind this partnership with them.

Mario Pierry: Clear. Are you the only bank in Latin America that has this partnership, or are you aware of this partnership of other banks?

João Vitor Menin: Yeah, as far as we know, we are the only bank in Latin America on this client advisory board with them. So, super excited with that.

Rafa Vitória: Thanks, João. This concludes our earnings conference call. Thank you all and see you next time.

#3194. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3192. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

Discover how Innomotics is driving the future of industry: https://www.innomotics.com/hub/en/company/about-innomotics/dynamo-electric-principle

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, plan restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

#3189. Security Bite: Apple details Secure Exclaves, a glimpse at its ambient computing future

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word.

Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

Much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

It’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.

Second, in October, we enrolled the 200th participant in ReMEDy2, our pivotal phase 2/3 trial in acute ischemic stroke. With this, we attained the prespecified enrollment threshold required for the REMEDY 2 interim analysis.

As a reminder, DM199 generic name rinbifetapenem alfa, is a recombinant form of human tissue kallikrein-1 or KLK1.

Through activation of the bradykinin-2 receptor pathway, we believe DM199 has the potential to improve vascular health and function. Ultimately improving blood flow. This is a completely novel mechanism of action and provides a common therapeutic rationale across preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, acute ischemic stroke, and other diseases. Even though the clinical objectives and endpoints differ across these indications. Let me begin with early onset fetal growth restriction program, or FGR. Professor Cluver has now completed enrollment in the first 2 cohorts of the phase 2 study being conducted at Tygerberg Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa. Together, these cohorts include 12 participants with 6 treated at 5 micrograms per kg and 6 treated at 10 micrograms per kg.

This is the first clinical evaluation of DM199 in women with early onset fetal growth restriction. Early onset FGR is a pregnancy disorder associated with significant risks to the fetus, frequently resulting from placental insufficiency. Creating impaired blood flow that restricts the supply of oxygen and nutrients to the baby. Currently, no therapy is approved to treat FGR. The only option today for physicians is to closely monitor both mother and baby balancing the risk of stillbirth and fetal complications from worsening placenta against the serious neonatal risk of delivering very prematurely. Pregnancies complicated by preeclampsia, maternal risk also includes severe high hypertension and organ injury.

The current early onset FGR study is evaluating repeated subcutaneous dosing of DM199 with the objective of assessing whether DM199 safely prolong pregnancy while minimizing risk to the mother and baby. Assessments include maternal and fetal safety, measures of utero placental vascular resistance, birth weight, centile, and duration of pregnancy. The dose for the third cohort will be selected based on the findings from the first 2 cohorts. On Tuesday, November 24 at 8 a.m. eastern time, we will host a virtual key opinion leader event focusing on fetal growth restriction featuring preliminary results from both completed cohorts.

Professor Cluver will be joined by Professor Steven Tong, and Professor Susan Walker, who are from the University of Melbourne, and Professor Andrew Shannon, from King's College London. The panel will discuss the treatment landscape and unmet need, the clinical rationale for DM199, and preliminary safety and clinical observations in the context of current maternal fetal medicine best practices. Within the investigation response of trial, 2 additional preeclampsia studies are expected to begin enrollment by the end of 2026. 1 comprised of up to 30 women with early onset preeclampsia receiving repeated subcutaneous dosing of DM199 until delivery. This is referred to as our part 2 of the study.

The second study will include up to 30 women with late onset or late stage preeclampsia, who are acutely hypertensive with delivery expected within 72 hours. Referred to as Part 1b. In the second study, patients will receive DM199 via continuous intravenous infusion which may provide insight into whether IV dosing of DM199 can help control severe hypertension. We believe every day matters for mom and baby. Switching to IV DM199 may enable further prolongation of pregnancy for these women beyond the sub q dosing. We are also advancing our company sponsored phase 2 program in early onset preeclampsia.

Health Canada authorized a protocol amendment to the open label phase 2 dose finding study in September and preparations continue to initiate enrollment at Canadian sites. Also plan to expand the study into the United Kingdom subject to regulatory authorization. In October, the study received conditional authorization from the European Medicines Agency or EMA with consideration for full approval after country specific ethical and site requirements, creating an opportunity for future European expansion. This trial is designed to evaluate approximately 30 patients with early onset preeclampsia across 3 dose levels. Drawing on the Part 1a preeclampsia experience, and emerging FGR observations.

Together, both of these studies will provide further information on dosing and pharmacologic activity in different clinical settings, allowing us to develop a dosing plan for use in larger preeclampsia trials. In The United States, our focus remains on addressing FDA's feedback regarding the nonclinical reproductive toxicology data to support an investigational new drug application or IND. To study DM199 in preeclampsia in the United States. Last quarter, we discussed FDA feedback indicating that our completed rat reproductive toxicology studies may be acceptable to support an IND. I am pleased to report that the in life portion of the study has been completed and DM199 was well tolerated by the animals. We expect the pharmacokinetics and pharmacologic results in the coming weeks. And once the report is complete, we plan to submit to the FDA. Our other major recent clinical milestone was an acute ischemic stroke. Where REMEDY 2 reached the enrollment threshold for its prespecified interim analysis.

Acute ischemic stroke, where a blood clot blocks blood flow to the brain, can cause profound lasting disability or death. Current reperfusion treatments including thrombolytic drugs, which attempt to dissolve the clot and mechanical thrombectomy, which attempts to physically remove the clot can be highly effective for certain eligible patients. But their use is limited by clinical eligibility, treatment time window, and the location of the clots. Most stroke patients either cannot receive these treatments or still experience significant disability despite treatment, is why stroke also remains a significant unmet medical need and additional approaches to preserve at-risk brain tissue. And improve functional recovery are urgently needed.

Following the required 90-day follow-up of the 200th participant, the independent data safety monitoring board, or DSMB, will examine the primary efficacy endpoint. The proportion of participants with a modified Rankin Scale score of 0 to 1 at day 90, indicating an excellent functional outcome. As part of the trial's prespecified adaptive design, the DSMB will use this efficacy data to determine whether the study should continue. And if so, whether the final sample size should be adjusted. If the trial continues, the final enrollment target will range from 300 to 728 participants under the prespecified statistical plan. Diomedical will remain blinded to the treatment effect data reviewed by the DSMB.

If successful, REMEDY 2 has the potential to serve as a pivotal trial supporting a future new drug application or NDA. For use of DM199 in acute ischemic stroke. Patient recruitment continues during the completion of the follow-up period and data preparations for interim review. We expect the DSMB to complete its analysis in the first quarter of 2027. With that, I will turn the call over to Julie to discuss the clinical programs in more detail. Julie?

Julie Krop: Thank you, Rick, and good morning, everyone. I would like to expand on 2 aspects of our pregnancy related development strategy. First, what are we seeking to learn from the FGR cohorts? And second, the initial preeclampsia findings are informing the next studies. Severe early onset fetal growth restriction presents a substantial challenge because impaired placental function can severely limit the fetus' ability to grow and develop As Rick noted, clinical management requires balancing the potential benefit of prolonging gestation against the maternal and fetal risk of continuing the pregnancy.

We are evaluating whether and to what degree DM199 can favorably affect vast vascular physiology to improve vascular health and blood flow and ultimately support improved outcomes for both the mother and the baby. The ongoing Phase 2 FGR IST trial is evaluating repeated subcutaneous dosing of DM199 in women with early onset disease. Key assessments include safety and tolerability, and umbilical artery Doppler indices, that reflect the degree of resistance to blood flow from the fetus to the placenta. Abnormal Doppler findings, particularly absent or reversed end diastolic flow, help guide the timing of delivery in pregnancies complicated by fetal growth restriction.

Changes in these physiologic parameters will provide important information about the pharmacologic activity of DM199 and help inform further development. At the November 24 KOL event, we will review preliminary observations from the 2 6-participant cohorts tested at DM199 subcutaneous dose levels 5 and 10 micrograms per kilogram, respectively. Although this is an early open label study involving a small number of patients, the findings will provide an initial opportunity to assess DM199 safety, pharmacologic activity, and potential clinical effects in women with early onset FGR. And importantly, the experts will help put the open label data into context by providing benchmarking data on outcomes in patients receiving current standard of care treatment.

In Part 1a of the investigator sponsored trial, patients with late onset preeclampsia were studied. If you recall, that data showed rapid and sustained reductions in maternal systolic and diastolic blood pressure following DM199 treatment. We also observed pharmacodynamic effects including trends suggesting reduction in the uterine artery pulsatility and a measure of resistance and an indirect measure of uteroplacental blood flow. Together, these observations support dose selection and provide a strong rationale for conducting additional studies to determine whether DM199 can deliver meaningful clinical benefits, particularly in early onset disease. I would also like to highlight the clinical rationale for DM199 in acute ischemic stroke. Unlike thrombolytic therapies, which dissolve blood clots or mechanical thrombectomy, which physically remove them.

DM199 is designed to improve collateral blood flow within the ischemic penumbra the surrounding brain tissue that are adversely impacted by the clot, and that remain viable for a period of time but are at risk of irreversible injury if adequate blood flow is not restored. By improving hospital delivery to the threatened tissue, we believe DM199 may help preserve neurologic function ultimately leading to improved recovery following stroke. REMEDY 2 is a randomized double blind placebo controlled study evaluating DM199 in patients with acute ischemic stroke who begin treatment within 24 hours of symptom onset. Participants receive DM199 or placebo over 3 weeks with functional recovery assessed at day 90.

The study focuses on patients who are not candidates for mechanical thrombectomy, a population with substantial unmet medical need. Across these programs, our goal is to determine whether DM199's effect on vascular function and blood flow can translate into meaningful clinical benefits for patients with these serious conditions. #3187. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, enabling ‘dot’ agents to make purchases

OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a new bar for secure payments by agents.”

ChatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet is the “first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users,” OpenAI explains, “so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.”

The feature won’t work with websites that block agents, however, which has increasingly become an issue online.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

You can read more about ChatGPT Wallet and how it works here.

The company emphasizes that payments are secure, card info isn’t shared with your dot or merchants, and that you’re in control of purchases.

#3186. iOS 27.2 has two CarPlay improvements, here’s what’s new

iOS 27.2 arrived last month with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users.

Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’

Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.

Like you would expect, ‘New Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.

This overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your shows and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a big fan of the change.

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app.

These changes are related to the broader rebrand of Apple Music that was recently unveiled.

For more new features in CarPlay that debuted in iOS 27, see our coverage here.

What are your favorite recent changes in CarPlay? Let us know in the comments.

#3184. ImmuCell (ICCC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Higher calf values and a new $8 million expansion fuel the growth.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

ImmuCell Corporation (ICCC +5.19%) reported a strategic shift toward its First Defense product line, exiting development of the Re-Tain mastitis treatment to prioritize bovine scours preventatives. Management indicated that high market values for beef and dairy calves supported increased demand for premium antibody products, driving top-line growth and improved manufacturing utilization. The company is executing an 8 million capital expansion project to alleviate manufacturing bottlenecks, specifically in freeze-drying and liquid processing, with completion targeted through late 2027. This transition included repurposing existing facilities and personnel to support First Defense production and sourcing capabilities.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the ImmuCell Corporation conference call to discuss unaudited third quarter 2026 financial results. All participants will be in a listen-only mode. I thank all of you for joining us today to discuss the unaudited earnings for the third quarter and nine months ended September 30, 2026. Listeners are reminded and cautioned that statements made by management during the course of this call include forward-looking statements, which include any statement that refers to future events or expected future results or predictions about steps the company plans to take in the future.
