With that said, let me turn the call over to Olivier te Boekhorst, President and CEO of ImmuCell Corporation, for some opening remarks. Olivier?

Olivier te Boekhorst: Thanks, Joe, and good morning, everyone. It's my pleasure to welcome you today to the discussion of ImmuCell's results for the third quarter of 2026. Our discussion of results will be accompanied by a few key slides that are also part of our updated investor presentation. You can find that on our investor page, immucell.com/investors. I will start off today's call with a quick summary of ImmuCell's strategy, which we have developed and refined over the past year. We made the decision in December of 2025 to focus exclusively on First Defense, our bovine scours preventative product line, to take advantage of attractive market tailwinds.

High calf values drive producer interest in effective preventatives, and we saw significant opportunity for growth in the U.S. and future international markets. We stopped investing in a new product for subclinical mastitis called Re-Tain, also driven by our contract manufacturer's inability to obtain GMP approval from the FDA. Our mission became to ensure we had sufficient supply to meet demand for First Defense and to restore our customers' confidence in that ability to supply after a protracted period of supply challenges leading to back orders. We invested in leadership, in expanding our commercial team, in colostrum sourcing capabilities, and importantly, in manufacturing. Our first imperative was to increase manufacturing yields to reliably produce more with existing equipment.

Then we followed that with a plan to invest $8 million to increase manufacturing capacity by the end of 2027. We are now looking more closely at improving our product costs and investing in longer-term growth strategies such as international expansion and innovation. The results this quarter, $8 million in revenue representing 46% growth compared to the third quarter of 2025, 44.2% gross margin, and $1 million net income compared to a $140,000 loss in the third quarter of 2025, tell us that our focus on First Defense is working.

Our results reflect the benefits of restored product availability, a favorable domestic calf market, increased commercial activity, and significant improvements in how we manage our supply chain from sourcing to processing colostrum. For a company our size, the singular focus on First Defense and managing our supply chain to support increasing customer demand continues to make a lot of sense, and we are excited to report on our progress today. I will now turn the call over to Timothy Fiori, our Chief Financial Officer, for a deeper review of our third quarter financial results. Tim?

Timothy Fiori: Thank you, Olivier. I will start with a short recap of product sales results, which are unchanged from our October 12th press release. All the numbers I will speak to are approximate and rounded. Product sales for the third quarter of 2026 came in at $8 million, an increase of 46% compared to the third quarter of 2025. The large year-over-year increase in the third quarter sales reflects, in part, the absence of distributor restocking headwinds that had adversely affected the third quarter sales in 2025. Domestic sales for the third quarter grew 29.2% compared to the third quarter of 2025 to $6.9 million, while international sales for the third quarter grew 573% to $1.1 million in the same period.

Sales to Canada accounted for the majority of international growth, boosted in large part by clearing of 2025 back orders. In the first nine months of this year, we achieved $25.6 million in product sales, a 27.8% increase compared to the first nine months of 2025. Tri-Shield, our flagship product that offers the most advanced protection against neonatal diarrhea, had strong 32.1% growth for the first nine months of 2026. We also assess commercial performance by looking at volume growth at the distributor level. In the first nine months of 2026, distributor volumes grew 23% compared to the same period last year, and 18% in the third quarter of 2026 compared to the third quarter of 2025.

Gross margin as a percentage of product sales was 44.2% in the third quarter of 2026, compared to 42.9% in the third quarter of 2025 and 33.9% in the second quarter of this year. The year-over-year increase in the third quarter primarily reflected higher pricing and improved manufacturing execution, partially offset by the shift of expenses formerly associated with Re-Tain into cost of goods sold. That is an important dynamic that I want to explain a bit more.

The shift of Re-Tain product development expenses to cost of goods sold due to the decision to repurpose the Re-Tain facility and equipment to First Defense resulted in approximately $400,000 of expenses being shifted to cost of goods sold, which reduces the Q3 stated gross margin by 480 basis points. The improvement sequentially from the second quarter of this year to the third quarter was primarily driven by increased manufacturing output across all departments, lower scrap, and greater benefits from product pricing. We are seeing benefits from our manufacturing yield improvement projects. Sales, marketing, and administrative expenses increased to $2.4 million in the third quarter of 2026 compared to $1.6 million in the third quarter of 2025.

This was driven by investments in leadership and expanded commercial activities, as previously announced and as Olivier will be discussing shortly. Product development expenses declined from approximately $700,000 in the third quarter of 2025 to approximately $175,000 in the third quarter of 2026, driven by reductions in spending on Re-Tain product development and the previously mentioned shift of former Re-Tain-related expenses to cost of goods sold. At this point in time, we are not planning any significant future spending on Re-Tain. To wrap up our income statement discussion, our net income was approximately $1 million during the third quarter of 2026, compared to a net loss of $140,000 in the third quarter of 2025.

For the first nine months of 2026, net income was $4.7 million compared to $1.8 million during the same period last year. The nine-month 2026 results include the one-time $2 million legal settlement received from our former contract manufacturer during the second quarter, and the nine months of 2025 results were augmented by a $427,000 insurance settlement. As usual, we provided adjusted EBITDA figures in yesterday's earnings release, together with a reconciliation against net income under GAAP. We believe that looking at adjusted EBITDA assists management and investors by looking at our performance across reporting periods on a consistent basis, excluding certain charges from our reported income before income taxes.

Adjusted EBITDA was $1.9 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared to $800,000 in the third quarter of 2025. For the first nine months of 2026, adjusted EBITDA was $7.3 million compared with $4.4 million during the same period last year. The nine-month year-to-date 2026 figure includes the aforementioned $2 million one-time legal settlement, and the nine-month 2025 results were augmented by the aforementioned $427,000 insurance settlement. To wrap up with financials, let me highlight a few key balance sheet items. Our balance sheet as of September 30, 2026, continues to be in a strong position with $7.9 million of cash on hand and $9.9 million of inventory.

We have started spending cash on the First Defense manufacturing capacity expansion, and I will speak more to that in a bit. We are very pleased at this time to be headed into what is typically our busy season with a finished goods inventory of around $3 million. Working capital increased from $13 million at the end of 2025 to $16.9 million at the end of the third quarter of 2026. The settlement contributed $2 million to our cash and working capital improvements.

You may have read in our press release that we are anticipating the signing of a new $3 million line of credit with a term of three years, which replaces our previous $1 million one-year term line of credit, which expired in September. Additionally, we have announced that we've notified our investment banking firm that we are terminating our at-the-market sales agreement, which has been unused since May of 2025 with no plans for use in the future. Historically, manufacturing capacity has been a constraint on ImmuCell's growth, so ensuring reliable supply remains a strategic priority. ImmuCell previously announced investments in freeze-drying and liquids processing capacity to build scalable manufacturing capabilities and ensure continued reliable supply of First Defense.

We mentioned in the last earnings call that during the first half of the year, our team completed an extensive planning process encompassing process design, equipment and facility requirements, cost estimates, and implementation planning. The resulting plan combines new equipment with our established expertise in preserving, concentrating, and purifying colostrum-derived antibodies. We are now at the beginning of the implementation process and have already ordered a lot of the key equipment. As of September 30, 2026, we had spent $1.7 million on the expansion project, mainly for the purchase of equipment. The construction process will be starting soon. We still expect to complete the initial phase of the expansion, which is freeze-drying, in the first half of 2027.

The liquids processing expansion is also on track and expected to be completed by the end of 2027. This overall project continues to be on track to our original $8 million overall budget. This level of expansion was made possible thanks to management decisions to repurpose our former Re-Tain® manufacturing facility and equipment. With that, I'll turn the call back to Olivier. Olivier?

Olivier te Boekhorst: Thanks, Tim, and congratulations to the entire team for an excellent quarter. As I mentioned in my initial remarks, ImmuCell made the decision in late 2025 to focus on our scours preventative products known as First Defense. The combination of factors led to this decision, and let me touch on calf values before discussing commercial activity and our new products. Our industry continues to benefit from historically strong calf values. Whether it's a calf born in a traditional beef herd or one originating on a dairy, their value has risen fivefold since 2021. Calf values are expected to remain strong in 2027 and 2028 as tight cattle supplies continue to underpin the market.

These higher calf values are reshaping farm-level economics, making newborn calf health an increasingly important priority. In addition, as dairies adopt more beef genetics to meet demand for beef, there are fewer dairy replacement heifers to support dairy herd expansion, which makes those heifers more valuable. For ImmuCell, this means that producers are interested to learn more about our premium products. The return on investment from using Tri-Shield has always been highly positive, even back in 2021 before calf values increased so dramatically. Certainly, protecting a calf worth more than $2,000 with a $15 product makes a lot of sense today.

Another driver for our top-line growth is our commercial activity, and we've made significant investments in our team and capabilities. Since last November, we have expanded our commercial team from nine to 13 people. The expanded sales team continues to increase customer engagement. As new hires gain traction in their territories, quality sales calls increased significantly from the second to the third quarter, and revenue per field sales representative also grew year-over-year. New customers contributed about 46% of our net growth in the third quarter of 2026, and increased utilization of existing customers contributed the remaining 54% of growth.

In the third quarter, dairy customers largely drove demand, as relatively few traditional cow-calf operations calve during this part of the year. This is great news for our business, as dairy demand tends to be stable from quarter to quarter. The last driver I will touch on is our new product line, Functional Feed. This line was developed for the calf ranch segment that we believe raises more than 4 million calves. Calf ranches manage large populations of primarily beef-on-dairy calves sourced from multiple farms that have varying newborn calf health protocols. Managing the inherent variability in these incoming calves that are two to seven days old when they arrive at the ranch can be a challenge.

Ideally, these calves benefited from Tri-Shield at birth, but that's difficult for the calf ranchers to determine. We developed a Functional Feed product line that is based on the same hyper-immunized colostrum we use for our biologicals line and is manufactured using a different and lower-cost drying technology. It has a much lower price per dose to encourage calf ranchers to administer it to all incoming calves. We have demonstrated 50% lower pre-weaning removal rates at these customers, which increases the number of calves that get to the market weight and generates a robust return on investment for the calf ranchers.

Although we do not report on this product line as a separate segment, we are very pleased to have met our full-year targets already and are optimistic about the runway for further growth. Sales of First Defense are recovering after setbacks related to contamination issues that created back orders. We estimate that First Defense captures about 34% of the spending on bovine scours biological products in the U.S., and we are very pleased with our premium positioning. Let me share this unsolicited remark from a dairy farmer on the Dairy Girl Network, an online community connecting women in the U.S. dairy industry. Quote, "For any lady struggling with newborn calf scours and loss, I highly recommend First Defense.

I am not a salesperson, but this stuff works. In seven months, we've only lost three out of 650 heifers born. This has been a miracle on our farm, and I wish someone would have told me about this years ago." End quote. These types of unsolicited endorsements remind us why we do what we do and drive our commitment to getting First Defense into the hands of more producers. Changes in our manufacturing process have been a key part of our performance year to date. In the past few years, we have worked to reduce the impact of bacterial contamination, and we have made great progress preventing scrap events.

Now, we have shifted our focus to managing yields to increase output. Ultimately, output drives our gross margin, given our relatively fixed manufacturing cost structure. So far in 2026, we have produced an average of about 435,000 manufacturing units per month. Manufacturing units are a standard measure we use to account for differences between Tri-Shield and Dual-Force products in our product line and are not the same as doses or revenue. Our average monthly output in 2026 has been 14% higher than 2025, and that compares to just 252,000 units per month in 2023 during the height of our contamination issues. Essentially, we now have a better understanding of our bottlenecks. We plan ahead to maximize their output.

We have changed our shift schedules to accommodate all these efforts, and we have made some changes to technology and equipment. While we look forward to bringing new equipment online for greater First Defense capacity by the end of 2027, we believe we can meet customer demand in the meantime with improved yield management. This quarter, we spent significant effort looking further back in our supply chain, specifically sourcing of colostrum and manufacture of the vaccines that we use to hyper-immunize the cows that give us the colostrum. We hired a team leader for our farm team, we developed a new value proposition for our source farms, and we are running trials to improve yields from the collected colostrum.

It is a competitive market for colostrum sourcing, and we are seeing an increase in prices. Nevertheless, our new value proposition and approach should improve our colostrum sourcing and increases our confidence in our ability to meet future demand. One final comment on Re-Tain. As we mentioned, we stopped investing in this new product development project. Recent clinical trials were unsuccessful in supporting incremental or new claims. We have entered into a minor licensing agreement with an aquaculture company for rights to use our intellectual property for certain marine species, and this may generate future cash flows. Throughout ImmuCell, we remain focused on First Defense and on strengthening process discipline and improving execution.

I want to thank the team, from sales to farm management to vaccine manufacturing and colostrum processing, and all the other functions that support the business, for their excellent work. It is a pleasure to work with the team as we execute our focused strategy to deliver today while we secure the future. With that said, we would be happy to take your questions. Let's have the operator open up the lines.

Operator: We will now begin the question-and-answer session. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your touch-tone phone. If you are using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. If at any time your question has been addressed and you would like to withdraw your question, please press star then two. At this time, we will pause momentarily to assemble our roster. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star then one to join the question queue. The first question today comes from Frank Gasker, a private investor. Please go ahead.

Frank Gasker: A very good quarter. What specifically changed between Q2 and Q3 to restore gross margins to 44%? Are those improvements sustainable?

Timothy Fiori: Hey, Frank. Thanks for your question. This is Tim. I would say the biggest driver was really the manufacturing volume. I mean, we did have a price change in August that helped a little bit as well. Our margins are fairly sensitive to output, and as we discussed in the Q2 call, we were doing some work on improving yields, and there were some experimentation going on in manufacturing. That definitely had an impact in Q2. In Q3, all the manufacturing teams, so we have vaccine, liquids manufacturing, and then formulation and fill are kind of the three primary legs of it, and they all had really good output for the quarter, and that helps a lot.

That is the primary driver, is just the change there.

Frank Gasker: Okay. With finished goods up 50% and work in progress actually down 15%, are we seeing permanent improvement in manufacturing throughput? How much additional demand, rather, can existing capacity support?

Olivier te Boekhorst: This is Olivier. Thank you for your follow-up question. We are seeing an increase in manufacturing throughput to the 435,000 manufacturing units per month on average, which is a 14% or so increase from last year. That explains both our gross margin, but it also is the result of some very specific yield improvement projects that we have implemented over the last, I would say, year or so to improve output. Could you repeat the second part of your question, please?

Frank Gasker: How much additional demand can existing capacity support?

Olivier te Boekhorst: That's a very good question as well, and it's somewhat of a moving target. We believe we can continue to improve manufacturing yields as we have been to meet demand until the new drying capacity expansion project has been completed, because drying is our current bottleneck in our process. As Tim discussed and showed on the slide, the new freeze dryer that we're planning to have installed in the first half of 2027, that should triple or so our capacity for freeze-drying. We are working towards achieving that big milestone. In the meantime, we believe we have enough capacity and further improvement potential to meet demand.

Frank Gasker: Thank you very much. I'll get back in the queue.

Operator: The next question comes from George Melas with MKH Management. Please go ahead.

George Melas: Good morning. Thanks for taking my question. Congratulations on really wonderful progress. I have a question on the mix between Tri-Shield and Dual-Force. Does the persistently high value of calves drive more Tri-Shield versus Dual-Force, and does that impact gross margins?

Olivier te Boekhorst: Thank you for your question, George. Happy to take this one. We do not comment on the gross margins of individual products, but I will say that, in general, Tri-Shield is priced higher. It also takes a little more effort to produce because there is a third, it protects against rotavirus, compared to Dual-Force that protects against corona and E. coli. Yes, with higher calf values, what it does, it makes it a little bit easier to get in front of the producer to have a conversation about how to protect these calves.

Then once you are in that conversation, it really depends on the producer's understanding of what is going on in their particular production, that then drives whether they will use one or the other product. Of course, we are focused on promoting Tri-Shield. We believe it provides the highest value to producers, and that is why you will see very healthy growth rates on that product line.

George Melas: Okay. Regarding the freeze-drying capacity, I believe you have four freeze dryers. How many are you adding, and what capacity expansion do you expect on the drying function?

#3183. Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving

iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:

I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find new places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

Even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden.

To find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a new ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

Trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen shows only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in New York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

How does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”

Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple says you’ll want to save any places you plan to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

It’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that says when it was last updated.

Have you used Local Lists in iOS 27’s Maps app yet? Let us know what you think via the comments.

#3181. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

#3180. Cathie Wood Goes Bargain Hunting: 3 Stocks She Just Bought

Three growth stocks trading sharply lower this year were on the Ark Invest shopping list on Thursday.

It's Friday the 13th, but Cathie Wood isn't scared. The widely followed growth investor has been busy adding to some of her favorite positions. The co-founder at Ark Invest bought more shares of Archer Aviation (ACHR -6.93%), CoreWeave (CRWV -6.13%), and Rocket Lab (RKLB -3.96%) on Thursday.

The three stocks are trading as much as 42% lower in 2026. Wood is buying on weakness, something that there have been plenty of opportunities to do so far this year. Let's take a closer look at all three transactions.

Turbulence has been part of the Archer Aviation stock ownership experience since going public via a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) in late 2021. The shares plummeted almost 70% in its first full year on the market, only to soar fourfold in value over the three subsequent years. That brings us to 2026, with investors losing altitude again. Archer has fallen 42% this year through Thursday's close.

Archer's goal is ambitious. It's one of two publicly traded players with 10-figure market caps that have developed electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. They are small and take off vertically like a helicopter, so they don't require long runways to take off and land. Some key differences from traditional helicopters are that they have much smaller propellers, fly more like small airplanes when airborne, and are electric.

The platform is viable. Archer is currently taking its flagship Midnight aircraft on the road, so to speak, in a "No Roads" flight tour. It is demonstrating its product as it clears the Federal Aviation Administration requirements ahead of passenger flights expected to start next year. Analysts see Archer's revenue taking off in a hurry in the coming years.

There are some limitations. Archer's Midnight can travel only 100 miles between charges. It also has enough room for just four passengers in addition to the pilot. There is still a market for these short trips in the luxury air-taxi and stealth military markets, and Archer has already lined up a few potentially lucrative deals on those fronts.

It will be years before it reaches profitability, but a strong balance sheet -- flush with more than $1.3 billion in cash -- gives it plenty of time to get there. Investors saw what happened to Archer stock the last time it had a sharp annual decline. Wood and her Ark Invest team believe it can happen again.

CoreWeave stock was one of this week's biggest earnings season gainers, soaring 25% on its heaviest trading volume of the year on Wednesday. It was a blowout performance, but the hyperscaler's stock is still trading more than 20% lower in 2026.

CoreWeave's revenue growth accelerated to 168% in this week's financial report, a big step up from the still-impressive 113% top-line jump it posted in the second quarter. It also raised its guidance. Its order backlog continues to swell.

The AI boom is still in play. CoreWeave mentioned on its call that demand for next year is 10 times its current capacity. It's a good problem for a company to have, but the sustainability of that momentum is what keeps the market nervous between the upticks. It doesn't mean that there aren't opportunities in the pockets of uncertainty. It probably helped CoreWeave this week that more than 13% of its shares are currently being sold short. A stronger-than-expected report like the hyperscaler delivered this week can send those bears scrambling to cover their positions.

Awarding Rocket Lab as the relative winner of this shopping list because it's only down 8% this year is deceptive. Rocket Lab shares are still 58% below their all-time high set just six months ago.

It doesn't mean that Rocket Lab isn't ready to take off again. It's a leading provider of space systems and launch services, at a time when rocket launches have never been more popular.

Revenue soared 73% to $268 million in its latest quarter. Its order backlog of $3.6 billion surged 52% in just the previous three months. Rocket Lab is also inching closer to profitability, reporting positive operating cash flow in the third quarter. Being further along the growth curve in the often-speculative universe of space stocks has its advantages.

When it comes to cleaning tasks, I’ve always relied on my trusted white vinegar to come to the rescue. Be it cleaning surface stains or giving my windows a streak-free finish, there are so many uses for white vinegar around the home.

But why exactly are people spraying vinegar on their front doors this season? While your first thought might be to simply clean the surface thoroughly, you’ll be mistaken.

According to a University of Minnesota Extension study, diluted white vinegar can deter pests like ants and spiders from taking refuge in your home. So all of a sudden, layering it on your front door makes sense. Here’s why.

It seems like white vinegar can do so much more than cleaning and limescale removal; it also makes a great natural ant and pest repellent. Not only do ants have a highly sensitive sense of smell and can be overwhelmed by the strong vinegar odor, but it can also clean up ant pheromone paths — disrupting them from guiding others toward food and moisture sources.

Essentially, spraying white vinegar eliminates the chemical scent trails ants leave behind, helping to prevent an infestation in your home. Which is why it’s a good idea to target potential entryways such as around the front door frame, baseboards, and cracks.

Essentially, spraying white vinegar eliminates the chemical scent trails ants leave behind, helping to prevent an infestation in your home.

Bear in mind that using vinegar is only a short-term fix rather than a long-term deterrent.

And this isn’t guaranteed to banish a persistent pest problem or a full infestation. In that case, it’s always best to call a professional local pest control service to handle it.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Simply mix equal parts white vinegar and water in a spray bottle to create a mild solution. Then, spray this mixture around your front door, making sure to target any small gaps or crevices where ants might enter. This process helps erase chemical trails left by ants and temporarily interrupts their activity. What’s more, it’s cheap, chemical-free, and only takes seconds to do.

Also, since white vinegar has a high acidity level, take care to protect nearby plants and sensitive surfaces from potential damage.

Alternatively, experts advise soaking cotton wool balls in peppermint essential oil before putting them around door frames. The strong fragrance will be too overpowering for such pests and will prevent them from entering.

This pure peppermint oil is paraben free, and provides a fresh scent. Versatile to use in aromatherapy, or in an oil or reed diffuser. And while the fragrance is pleasant to our senses, it is also known to be a natural pest repellent.

For more pest tips, be sure to clear this one thing in their yard to prevent rats this fall.

NOTE: Do NOT use peppermint oil if you have pets as this is toxic when inhaled or ingested.

#3177. iOS 27.3 adds three new features I’ve used almost every day

iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day.

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Read more: iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:

The updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this update.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

Read more: watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

Which new iOS 27.3 features have you been enjoying in the beta? Let us know in the comments.

#3176. Prairie Op. Co. (PROP) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

October output peaked, then natural decline set in.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Prairie Operating Co. (PROP +13.93%) reported increased production and revenue for the third quarter, supported by the completion of 37 wells across five pads. Management stated that development activity at the Burnett and Castor pads validated acreage quality and facilitated the conversion of potential locations into proved undeveloped inventory. The company reported a reduction in unit operating costs and highlighted the integration of internal logistics to improve margins. While production reached a peak in early October, the company emphasized disciplined capital allocation and a focus on generating free cash flow to improve its liquidity position by year-end.

Operator: Good morning and welcome to the Prairie Operating Co.'s third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Today's call is being recorded. At this time, I'd like to turn the call over to Wobbe Ploegsma, Vice President of Investor Relations and Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

Wobbe Ploegsma: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining Prairie Operating Co.'s third quarter 2026 earnings call. Before we provide our prepared remarks, I would like to remind all participants that our comments today will include forward-looking statements, which are subject to certain risks, uncertainties, and assumptions. Actual results could differ materially from those expressed or implied by these forward-looking statements. Additionally, we may refer to non-GAAP financial measures. For a more detailed discussion of the risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially, as well as reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures, please refer to the company's earnings release and public filings, including our Form 10-Q for the quarter ending September 30th, 2026.

These materials, along with an updated investor presentation, are available on our website. Joining me today are Greg Patton, Chief Executive Officer, and Michael Shelly, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. With that, I'll turn the call over to Greg.

Greg Patton: Thanks, Wobbe, and good morning. Development program. Average daily sales volumes increased 19% from the prior quarter to 26,117 BOE per day, and we exited the quarter at 30,229 BOE per day. Revenue grew 31% from the prior quarter to $129.5 million. We have completed a large portion of our 2026 capital plan, bringing 37 wells across five pads online to date, adding to our stronger production base and generating greater confidence in the opportunities ahead. Third quarter sales volumes totaled approximately 2.4 million BOE, an increase of 21% from the prior quarter, with 77% liquids, including 56% oil.

For the first nine months, sales volumes totaled approximately 6.5 million BOE, or approximately 23,730 BOE per day, with 74% liquids, including 52% oil. Production momentum continued into early October. As a result of the wells turned in line during the third quarter, production continued to increase, reaching approximately 32,287 BOE per day by early October. Our current results are supported by the execution of our development program. Year to date, we have drilled 27 wells across four pads, with 19 wells drilled in a single run. These wells averaged approximately 18,700 feet in measured depth, at an average rate of penetration of 380 ft per hour, and an average spud to rig release time of 6.2 days.

We have completed 37 wells over five pads, consisting of 27 Niobrara and 10 Codell, with the last three new pads coming online in the third quarter, all above type curve. We are currently in the process of drilling four additional wells that will come online in 2027. At Castor, completion activities on the six-well pad were finalized in September, with the wells coming online at the end of the month, predominantly contributing to the fourth quarter production. Turning to Burnett, the four-well development came online at the end of August and represents an important milestone in demonstrating the value of Prairie's acreage.

The wells were drilled across three distinct drilling and spacing units, including two 1,280-acre units and one 1,920-acre unit. The wells achieved an average maximum initial production rate of approximately 722 BOE per day per well, with an 81% oil cut on a two-stream basis, and generated cumulative gross production of 131,490 BOE through October 20th of this year. By drilling section line wells across each DSU, we demonstrated the consistent reservoir quality and reserve potential of the acreage while securing all three units for future development.

These early production results materially de-risked and validate the quality and future development potential of our acreage within the 5,700-acre Genesis OGDP I, and supported the conversion of 30 gross possible locations to proved undeveloped locations, expanding our proved inventory, reinforcing the commercial potential of nearby undeveloped locations, and reducing uncertainty around our near-term development program. We plan to return to each of these DSUs in the future drilling programs to complete their development. As we look ahead to the continued development of these DSUs and the broader Genesis OGDP I, the infrastructure already in place positions us to efficiently accommodate future production growth.

Our existing pipeline network provides reliable production flow and long-term takeaway flexibility, with oil, natural gas, and water connections that allow production to move off location without trucking, reducing operating costs, facility requirements, and environmental impacts. Our commercial agreements support and provide flexibility to our development plan, as well as support our artificial lift strategy. The existing infrastructure has been designed with sufficient capacity to maintain flow assurance throughout our future development program. In addition to de-risking acreage, infrastructure capabilities, and production growth, we continue to improve operating efficiencies.

Lease operating expense declined to $5.71 per meaningful cost efficiencies following the complete integration of the Bayswater operations, and remain focused on sustaining and extending those efficiencies across our larger production base. For example, during the quarter, we established Stagecoach Logistics LLC to bring field maintenance, logistics, and operational support functions in-house, reducing our reliance on third-party service providers. Centralizing these activities enables us to better control costs, equipment, and inventory while improving response times and field execution. Together, these initiatives help reduce LOE per BOE and demonstrate the operating leverage available across our expanded asset base. We will continue to focus on sustaining field-level efficiencies as we manage our larger producing base.

With our recently developed wells now online, our priorities are well performance, operating efficiency, and disciplined capital allocation. We believe the progress across our producing base provides a foundation for continued value creation. I will now turn the call over to Michael to review our financial results, liquidity, and capital structure.

Michael Shelly: Thanks, Greg. Good morning, everyone. Third quarter revenues totaled $129.5 million, up 31% from the prior quarter, including $114 million of oil revenue. For the first nine months, revenue reached $311.8 million, an increase of 97% year-over-year, and adjusted EBITDA totaled $136.4 million, an increase of 37% year-over-year. Prairie generated $65.3 million of adjusted EBITDA in the third quarter, an increase of 92% from the prior quarter, as sales volumes increased and unit operating costs declined. With Burnett and Castors now producing, our focus is on realizing the cash returns from the capital invested this year and carefully managing the spending required to sustain that production. Net loss attributable to Prairie was $48.9 million for the quarter.

After preferred stock dividends and remeasurement adjustments, net loss attributable to common stockholders was $34 million, or $0.26 per basic share and $0.28 per diluted share. The GAAP result includes $105.7 million of unrealized derivative losses, a $13.1 million fair value gain on financial instrument liabilities, and $18.4 million of income tax benefit. Average realized prices, excluding derivatives, were $84.48 per barrel of oil, $24.28 per barrel of NGLs, and $1.05 per MCF of natural gas. Including realized derivative settlements, prices were $62.24, $19.98, and $2.14, respectively. Net cash provided by operating activities was $123.4 million for the first nine months.

On a per BOE basis, lease operating expense was $5.71, transportation and processing expense was $1, ad valorem and production taxes were $4.96, and G&A was $4.56, which represents a 24% decrease compared to the prior quarter. At September 30, we had $7.8 million of cash and $3 million available under our reserve-based credit facility. The borrowing base and elected commitments were $475 million, with $472 million outstanding. During the quarter, we extended the Series F anniversary warrant issuance date to December 1, 2026.

We continue to pursue opportunities to refinance the remaining Series F preferred stock as part of our broader effort to strengthen Prairie's balance sheet, improve financial flexibility, and better align our capital structure with the scale of our operations. Our commodity swaps extend into 2029. Fourth quarter 2026 oil swaps covered approximately 1.37 million barrels at $63.23 per barrel, and natural gas swaps covered approximately 4.3 million MMBtu at $4.09 per MMBtu. These contracts provide downside protection. Our objective is to support Prairie's operating momentum through disciplined financial management and capital allocation that creates sustainable long-term shareholder value. With that, I will turn the call back to Greg for closing remarks.

Greg Patton: Thanks, Michael. With the recent results of the Burnett pad demonstrating the quality of our acreage, it has validated our development area and expanded our proved undeveloped inventory. Across Prairie, our team is focused on translating that operating progress into cash generation and long-term shareholder value. As we move through the remainder of 2026, our priorities are consistent: sustain well performance, maintain operating efficiencies, and allocate capital with discipline. On behalf of the board and management team, I want to thank our employees for their continued dedication and execution, and our shareholders for their ongoing support. With that, I will turn the call back over to the operator for Q&A.

Operator: Thank you. At this time, we will begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. Our first question is from the line of Leo Mariani with Roth. Please proceed with your questions.

Leo Mariani: Hey, guys. Just wanted to touch base on your CapEx here. So it looks like you have spent about $185 million in the first three quarters, which is the low end of the full-year budget. What do you see CapEx coming in at in Q4, given that you only have about $10 million left to kind of hit the high end of your budget? Just trying to get a sense of that.

Greg Patton: Morning, Leo. Glad to have you on the call this morning, and thanks for joining us. The number you're looking at obviously is on the cash flow statement, I'm assuming, is the 185. Ultimately, that is our cash out the door. The CapEx for the year is actually at about 165 in terms of our D&C CapEx for the year, so that leaves more of that 15-30 range on the rest of the year. As the remarks stated, we have four wells that we are drilling or are about to drill for the year. As we think about D&C costs on a gross basis, four wells, that's roughly with rig move and demove under that kind of $8 million marker.

As we're looking at $165 million of D&C costs, some ancillary costs still trickling in and around the final completions in the third quarter, coupled with that D&C capital and some other one-off projects here and there, we still feel strongly about our guidance range that was previously given of the 180-195. That being said, there are some inflationary expenses, albeit we had a lot of our products locked in for the year, particularly sand and steel products.

There will be some inflationary aspects that we have seen at the end of the third quarter with costs coming in, and as we get into the drilling expenses here in the fourth quarter, we are seeing some higher costs in and around those products.

Leo Mariani: Okay, I appreciate that. I guess, what do you guys see as kind of rough 2 mi lateral or well cost these days as a result of the inflation?

Greg Patton: That's a great question. Ultimately, as we look at the D&C costs we've talked about before exhibiting that kind of $5.3 million-$5.5 million range, those numbers have gone up. We're seeing $300,000-$500,000 of additional costs, and that could continue to go up depending on the geopolitical environment. What we would say would be not this round of drilling costs for the steel, but as we look at Q1 for the year and as we're looking at our programs pushing into 2027 and starting that process, it's a little bit of an unknown. We've seen a dramatic reduction in oil costs here recently. We've seen a dramatic increase in the number of ships coming through the strait.

We've seen a dramatic increase in imports coming in. The cost increases could hold flat at that $300,000-$500,000 kind of typical increase, or we could see more or less. It's a little bit of an unknown, so we're watching that very closely.

Leo Mariani: Okay, that makes sense. On your production, obviously you had a nice increase in Q3, but significant momentum on the production heading into Q4. You guys disclosed an early October rate, which looked very strong here at 32,300 barrels a day. Is that rate kind of holding here now that we're about a month later into kind of mid-November? Are you starting to see that kind of rate come off? Where do you think you're going to kind of end up in the end of the year? Is production kind of declining, and are we going to be lower than that 32,000 and change here in Q4?

Greg Patton: I'm not going to speak to Q4 quarterly guidance, but I will talk about general dynamics and economics of DJ horizontal laterals. 32,000 barrels a day, obviously in October, as we mentioned in our script, and as we think about the wells that came online that supported that with public data, obviously being the Burnetts and the Castors. As we look towards the back of the year from this point forward, production has held very strong, but there's obviously some natural decline as well. When we look at 32,000 barrels a day, that number has declined over the past 60 days, being the whole month of October, the month of November.

As we continue to move forward, ultimately we feel very supportive of our guidance at 23,000-25,000 BOEs per day on the annualized average. We feel very strong about the performance of our well bores. Natural decline is a thing, so I would not tell you that we would be exiting the year at 32,000 barrels a day, but also we're not guiding to what that exit rate production is at this time.

Leo Mariani: Good, that makes sense. Then just on liquidity, certainly looked a little bit tight here at September 30 with the cash and kind of the limited balance on the revolver, somewhere around $11 million of liquidity. Could you give us a perspective on, you think that improves quite a bit? It sounds like CapEx is coming down a lot in Q4 and production's strong. Do you expect considerable free cash flow here in Q4?

Michael Shelly: Hey, Leo, I'll answer that. You kind of hit the nail on the head there. With production being very strong and kind of limited CapEx here in the fourth quarter, our liquidity position will continue to improve fairly dramatically as we get into the end of Q4.

Leo Mariani: Okay, that makes sense. Just on the Series F preferred, I guess the deadline's coming for a warrant, anniversary warrant trigger here, I guess at the end of the month here. Do you guys feel like you might have to extend this again, or you think that you might be able to get something done here by December 1?

Greg Patton: Great question again, Leo. As you are very well aware and close to the matter, as we've talked about this a lot over the past year, is we've built a really strong relationship with High Trail. They've been a good partner with us as we've grown and expanded the business. They've been supportive of us through several amendments to push that anniversary warrant out. As we approach the December 1st aspect that you just mentioned, ultimately with the issuance of that anniversary warrant upon us, we are in discussions with High Trail. We are obviously reporting very good results as part of the quarterly call here. As we look towards what the next steps are, we're obviously evaluating many things.

We're very supportive of working with High Trail, and they're supportive of our development plan. We believe that an outcome will be available to us, and we'll be able to talk more about that as part of the year-end results.

Operator: Our next question is from the line of Charles Meade with Johnson Rice. Please proceed with your questions.

Charles Meade: Good morning, Greg and Michael, and the rest of the Prairie team there. Greg-

Charles Meade: I want to ask about. Yeah, thank you. I want to ask about the Burnett pad, and I wonder if you could talk about, I guess, two major dimensions of it. Number one, those results were strong to me, but I wanted to see if you could talk about how those came in versus maybe your internal base case or high side case. Then also, because this is a relatively, I guess, more recently tested area of the DJ, I wonder if you could also talk about how it compares to some of the results from the offset operators that have been drilling around you in the last year or so.

Greg Patton: Yeah, absolutely. Happy to, Charles. The Burnett pad is, first and foremost, was the original inception acreage behind Prairie Operating, dating back to 2023. That was the first acquisition that was utilized as part of the change in the structure from a crypto company into an oil and gas company on Nasdaq. Also our first original OGDP. As we looked to develop the acreage, there was a lot of stepping stones we had to get through in terms of pad development, takeaway midstream, et cetera, and so forth. We were very happy to be able to bring that online in the third quarter.

We developed it in a manner, testing the boundaries of that OGDP, and we did that intentionally, because ultimately, as you step into a new area, it's a little bit of a step out. Ultimately, you want to understand your geology, your economics, and the engineering, let alone just how that well's going to flow, and the dynamics of how it interacts with your midstream systems. We developed it in a manner that I would say is very conservative. We also developed it in a manner that we can go back and drill out the rest of that OGDP in several additional visits. Very excited about how we were able to do that and get to it.

We've talked about this area before. It sits between the Hereford Field and the Northeast Extension. As we look at historical operators in this area, you have Chevron, which was originally the original Noble acreage. You have Bison, you had Mallard, you had others that operated in and amongst these areas. We are definitely not first inventors here. We are fast followers. Your second question led to offset results, and how we compare. Ultimately, we are followers, and there are others that are seeing and exhibiting equal and/or better results than we are. We are definitely paying very close attention to the flowback methodology.

We are paying very close attention to the frac designs, et cetera, and so forth, so that as we are developing into these newer areas for us, not Greater Wattenberg, where the majority of our acreage sits, and have been very pleased with the results. I will end on the results, which was the last part of your question. Internally, they have beat our internal type curve results, both from an initial IP rate as well as from a cum rate at this point in time. We are being very diligent with these well bores in terms of the flowback methodology, in terms of the continued production results.

We look forward to continue to develop in this area and continue to use newer technologies, as many of our offsetting peers are using, to continue to enhance the development in this particular area and zone.

Charles Meade: Got it. That is great detail, Greg. Thanks. A quick follow-up on the 4Q production trajectory. Do you have any other wells that you are scheduled to bring online between now and year-end, or completions and TILs, are they done for the year at this point?

Greg Patton: The drilling schedule, as we announced, and as we are drilling wells, obviously there is a whole another 45 days ahead of us till the end of the year. The drilling results and DUCs available to be able to generate production would be very limited at this point in time. Most of the activity from this point forward would be benefiting Q1.

Charles Meade: Right. Okay, great. Thanks, Greg.

Operator: Our next questions are from the line of Jeff Robertson with Water Tower Research. Please proceed with your questions.

Jeff Robertson: Thank you. Good morning, Greg. To further the production trajectory, I think you mentioned the four wells that are in progress now will be on sometime in 2027. Can you share any color on how you see development maybe for the first couple of quarters of 2027 with new well completions?

Greg Patton: Jeff, at this point in time, we're not issuing 2027 guidance. I will tell you that the team has a robust amount of permits in hand, as evidenced by our reserve report. And we have initial kind of plans in place, and we're being proactive about what that first quarter will look like via those wells that we are drilling and having ready for completions in the fourth quarter. But at this point in time, the quantum and number of wells, which wells they will be, et cetera and so forth, we're not disclosing that yet.

Jeff Robertson: Michael, on the balance sheet, with the expectation of free cash flow growing in the fourth quarter of 2026, can you talk a little bit about balance sheet management between working capital and paying down the RBL?

Michael Shelly: Yes. As you expect, as cash flow continues to come in, we continue to pay our payables, which will lower our net working capital balance. At the same time, we will continue to pay down our RBL as well, as available. It is kind of tomato from my perspective, whether we are thinking about payables or paying down debt. But the point being that our liquidity position continues to improve as we exit the year.

Jeff Robertson: When is the next scheduled redetermination on the RBL?

Michael Shelly: We have quarterly redeterminations, so we are in the middle of a redetermination now. In terms of timing of that, expect some perspective on that in, let's say, December.

Jeff Robertson: Lastly, on the RBL, Michael, I believe there are some minimum production thresholds. Can you share any color on what the capital program needs to look like to meet those thresholds?

Michael Shelly: Yeah. Practically speaking, those production metrics have, of course, been met to date and will continue to be met based on our current production and our cash flow. I think from that perspective, there is no incremental development required in the near term to meet those production targets.

Operator: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, this will conclude today's question and answer session, and will also conclude today's conference. We thank you for your participation. You may disconnect your lines, and have a wonderful day.

The Galaxy S26 Plus is also available, with a larger 6.7-inch display and bigger battery. It's now $700, down from the usual $1,200.

The Motorola Razr 2026 is the ultimate cheap foldable, especially at this price. With it you get a pair of 50MP cameras, the foldable clamshell design with a 3.6-inch cover display, a 6.9-inch internal display, strong performance and a whopping 4.800 mAh battery pack. Perfect for anyone wanting a foldable experience on a budget.

The Pixel 11 Pro comes with an even brighter display, better cameras and battery life, a new HiLight notification alert and all the same benefits as the regular Pixel 11.

If you want a larger screen, the Pixel 11 Pro XL is the exact same phone, only bigger and with a larger battery. It's discounted from $1,299 to $794 at Mint.

The flagship Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is $500 off at Mini, offering four excellent cameras, a bright 6.9-inch display, strong battery life, S Pen support, and access to everything Galaxy AI has to offer.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is the foldable option, and while the discount isn't as generous it's a great way to get this phone for a slightly cheaper price. With it you get a large and bright 8-inch display, good cameras, Gemini automation support, a teleprompter mode and the unique Bubbles multitasking that trumps most other devices.

Foldables don't seem to offer much in the way of discounts at Mint, and the Galaxy Z Flip 8 is no exception. With $200 off, you get a compact phone that opens up into a 6.9-inchy display. You also get a pair of main cameras, a 4.1-inch cover display capable of running full Android apps, and access to Galaxy AI tools.

You also save $200 on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which comes with the popular new passport-shaped design. While we've seen the price of this phone get lower, you still get to enjoy a 7.6-inch folding display with anti-glare coating, a pair of 50MP cameras, and a sizable 4,800 mAh battery. Plus Galaxy AI and all the things that make a Samsung phone worth having.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has all the benefits of the Z Fold 8, but with more added extras. That includes a triple-lens camera system, a taller and larger pair of displays and an even bigger battery. If you want a foldable with a more book-like design, this is the one for you.

#3174. Perplexity brings AI agents feature called Teammates to the Mac

This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web.

Similar to Grok Bot, Perplexity Teammates are task-oriented proactive agentic AI threads that work for you without constantly being prompted. Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots are similar, but use a single chat model rather than supporting multiple instances.

Teammates are a team of AI agents that own ongoing work. Give a teammate a responsibility, such as managing a growth campaign, triaging incoming bug reports, tracking your metrics, or researching a new market, and it owns that work around the clock. It plans the tasks, brings in more agents when the work grows, and follows through until the result is ready for your review.

Access to Teammates currently requires a paid Perplexity Max subscription. The feature builds on top of Perplexity’s existing AI orchestration system.

#3173. How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program offers ethics and compliance training

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3172. Apple releases tvOS 27.2.1 and HomePod 27.2.1, here’s what’s new

Apple has just released tvOS 27.2.1 for Apple TV 4K and HomePod 27.2.1 for HomePod models, here’s what’s new.

Two new software updates arrived today for Apple Home devices:

tvOS 27.2.1 is the latest update for Apple TV 4K. And while the version numbering might make it appear very minor, it introduces a major new feature: Siri AI support.

Siri AI arrived as part of today’s Apple TV 4K (4th gen) launch. But as confirmed by this support document, the new Siri is also now available on select older Apple TV 4K models (2nd gen and 3rd gen) via tvOS 27.2.1.

tvOS 27.2.1 also includes a variety of security fixes.

We don’t yet have details on the changes introduced in HomePod 27.2.1. Apple’s release notes only say: “This update provides bug fixes.” When HomePod mini 2 launched late last month, Apple said Siri AI would arrive via a future software update, so today’s 27.2.1 release might be that update.

However, without any prior announcement from Apple, it seems more likely that the software simply includes bug fixes and performance updates for HomePod. We’ll keep you posted on what we find.

Update: Leaker pdfu has confirmed Siri AI is not included in HomePod 27.2.1.

Freshen up your Paramount+ watchlist with this trio of excellent arrivals

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Paramount+ has a really strong November 2026 library. Honestly, this is one of the hardest round-ups I’ve had to write in a while, such is the quality of film that’s gracing the streamer’s platform this month. While scrolling through the dozens of movies that have been added should be less of a chore for you than usual, I’m still here with three picks of flicks I’m confident you’ll thoroughly enjoy.

I can say with all sincerity that I genuinely love the three movies below. The first is a true romantic classic with a killer ending tune. The second is a film I love in part because of video game reasons, and also because it’s got Owen Wilson in rare ass-kicking mode. And the third? Well, that might genuinely be my favorite ever comedy, and it’s a flick that helped skyrocket a young Eddie Murphy to superstardom.

These are the three new to Paramount+ movies I recommend you drop everything to stream this weekend.

I won’t lie. At least half the reason I adore this iconic romantic drama is because of Jennifer Warnes and Joe Cocker’s “Up Where We Belong”. It’s an all-timer of a weepy tune. Oh, and the fact that “The Simpsons” also does an awesome parody of the movie’s classic ending in the season one episode, “Life on the Fast Lane”. Regardless of those factors, this is hands down Richard Gere’s best movie in my book.

Gere plays Zack Mayo, a hot-headed young punk with a heart who ends up joining the U.S. Navy Aviation Officer Candidate School… mainly to spite his alcoholic dad (Robert Loggia). Boot camp life proves a shock to the system for Mayo, especially because of his incredibly demanding Gunnery Sergeant Emil Foley (a never-better Louis Gossett Jr.). Along the way, he meets local mill worker Paula (Debra Winger), and they quickly develop a deep affection, in spite of the fact Mayo’s navy buddies believe she’s only looking to use him to escape small-time life. Just a wonderful all-round love story.

Watch “An Officer and a Gentleman” on Paramount + now

Owen Wilson in oh-so-rare action-star form. You gotta love it. There are two reasons why I'm a little bit obsessed with this incredibly solid action-thriller. Reason the First: that all-time banger by Feeder, “Buck Rodgers,” that plays early in the movie (I was playing a lot of Gran Turismo 3: A-Spec back in 2001). Reason number two: the relentless tracker Sasha Ivanić, who ruthlessly hunts Wilson’s Lt. Chris Brunett after his plane is shot down over war-torn Bosnia territory. Why? Because his tracksuit and general look definitely inspired Niko Bellic’s design in 2008’s Grand Theft Auto IV. Hey, I’m a geeky gamer who loves movies. Sue me.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The premise of “Behind Enemy Lines” is pretty simple. Our hero is shot down during a reconnaissance mission, but not before accidentally taking snaps of a mass grave that Serbian General Miroslav Lokar (Olek Krupa) definitely doesn’t want shared. Cue Brunett being forced to flee enemy troops for most of the movie’s runtime. Thankfully he’s got some support back at his aircraft carrier in the shape of the magnificently named Rear Admiral Leslie Reigart (Gene Hackman). This is a properly nail-biting flick with a relatively straight-laced turn from Wilson that I kind of wish we got to see more often.

Watch “Behind Enemy Lines” on Paramount + now

This is legit one of my favorite comedies of all time… and definitely one my old man let me watch too young as a kid. Let’s just say there’s a scene with Jamie Lee Curtis’ Ophelia (a sex worker with a big heart) that I certainly shouldn’t have been seeing as a young teenager. Anyway, this is unquestionably one of the best comedies of the ‘80s for me, and a film that put Eddie Murphy on the map even before 1984’s “Beverly Hills Cop”. In terms of director John Landis’ filmography, only 1981’s “An American Werewolf in London” can top “Trading Places”.

What is this caper actually about, you ask? It’s a tale of switched identities. The lives of Billy Ray Valentine (Murphy), a broke con artist, and wealthy managing director Louis Winthorpe (a brilliant Dan Aykroyd) are swapped on the whims of the scheming Duke Brothers. Why? Simply because these millionaires enjoy ruining lives, and all for the grand bet of a single dollar. Admittedly, there’s some stuff in that third act train scene that hasn’t aged particularly well, but this is still a comedy I hold huge affection for.

Dave was a computing editor at Tom’s Guide who covered everything from cutting edge laptops to ultrawide monitors. Now he contributes to the site in a freelance capacity. When he’s not worrying about dead pixels, Dave enjoys regularly rebuilding his PC for absolutely no reason at all. In a previous life, he worked as a video game journalist for 15 years, with bylines across GamesRadar+, PC Gamer and TechRadar. Despite owning a graphics card that costs roughly the same as your average used car, he still enjoys gaming on the go and is regularly glued to his Switch. Away from tech, most of Dave’s time is taken up by walking his husky, buying new TVs at an embarrassing rate and obsessing over his beloved Arsenal.
